path.summary: Most first-time PMs think the job is writing JIRA tickets and chairing standups. The job is actually translation and sequencing — taking a vague founder ask and turning it into a thing engineers can build, users can love, and sales can sell. By the end of this path you can scope a stakeholder request, run a real user interview, write a one-page PRD, prioritize a backlog, build a quarterly roadmap, ship a feature, and measure whether it worked.

lessons.title: What a PM Actually Does
lessons.subtitle: You're not the boss of engineering; you're the translator between rooms

audioChapters.label: Mental model: PM as translator and sequencer

blocks.md:
On day one, every new PM thinks the job is to write JIRA tickets, run standups, and chase engineers. By month six, the good ones realise the job is something else entirely.

The job is **translation** — converting a vague founder ask into a thing engineers can build, a thing users will adopt, and a thing sales can sell. And **sequencing** — deciding what gets built first, second, and never. Tickets and standups are the byproduct, not the work.

If you remember nothing else from this course, remember this: a PM with a great roadmap and no translation skill ships features nobody uses. A PM with translation skill and no roadmap ships nothing — but at least nobody is angry.

blocks.title: Mental model: PM is a translator plus a sequencer
blocks.md:
Picture three rooms — **Users**, **Engineers**, **Sales/CEO**. Each room speaks a different language and has different incentives. The PM is the door between them; the PM's value is whatever loss in translation they prevent.

Then, on top of that, the PM is the **sequencer**. Given finite engineers and infinite asks, the PM decides which ask gets built this sprint, which gets built next quarter, and which gets a polite no. Translation makes the asks legible. Sequencing makes them shippable.

blocks.caption: Watch one user complaint turn into an engineering ticket, a sales talking point, and a no-thank-you to a different stakeholder — all in the same week.

hi-IN.title: Priority ka asli scene
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. CEO ne bola **'Priority 1'**. PM ne meeting mein likha **'Priority 1.5, but really P1'**. Engineer ne JIRA mein likha **'P3, looks like a nice-to-have'**. Designer ne bola **'Yeh next quarter ka hai na?'**

Sab same ticket pe baat kar rahe hain. Aur ticket pe likha hai *'TBD'*. Yahi hai PM ka dard — 4 logon ki same ticket pe 4 alag understanding.

en.title: Priority drift, in one act
en.md:
The CEO calls it P1. The PM writes 'P1.5, but really P1' in the doc. The engineer files it as P3. The designer asks if it's next quarter's work. All four are looking at the same ticket. The ticket says 'TBD'.

This is the PM's daily problem in one sentence: same words, four meanings, zero alignment.

blocks.md:
**Output** is what you ship. **Outcome** is what changes for the user. Most PMs measure themselves on output because output is countable: features shipped, tickets closed, sprints completed. But shipping a feature nobody uses is not progress. It's debt.

A Bengaluru SaaS I worked with shipped 47 features in one year. Their DAU/MAU was 0.14. The CEO was proud of the velocity. The CEO was wrong. They had built a museum of features, not a product.

The move is to **state every initiative as an outcome before you state it as an output**. Not 'ship the new invoicing module' — that's an output. Try 'reduce time-to-first-invoice from 4 days to under 1 day for new SMB customers'. Now you can tell, three months later, whether it worked. The module is one possible answer; the outcome is the actual question.

blocks.title: Translating an output into an outcome — a worked example

steps.label: Step 1 — The original ask
steps.body: CEO Slack: 'We need to build a referral program.' This is an output disguised as a strategy. Six engineers could spend two months on it and you would still not know if it worked.

steps.label: Step 2 — Find the implied user behavior
steps.body: Ask: what behavior change would make the CEO happy? Probably 'more new signups from existing customers without us paying Google.' Now you have a direction.

steps.label: Step 3 — Pick a measurable target
steps.body: Frame it: 'Increase organic signups attributed to existing-customer referral from 4 percent to 12 percent of monthly new signups, by end of Q2.' Specific. Measurable. Time-boxed.

steps.label: Step 4 — Then, and only then, brainstorm outputs
steps.body: Now you can compare options: a referral code, a friend-invite flow, a public testimonials page, a customer-advocacy program. Each is a hypothesis about how to move the outcome. The cheapest one to test wins.

steps.label: Step 5 — Ship the cheapest test, measure, decide
steps.body: Ship a copy-link referral in 1 sprint. Measure for 4 weeks. If the metric moves, double down. If not, kill it before you build the loyalty programme that the CEO actually pictured.

hi-IN.title: Standup ka satya
hi-IN.md:
Standup mein PM bola: *'Aaj kya kar rahe ho?'* — Engineer 1: *'API integrate.'* Engineer 2: *'Bug fix.'* Engineer 3: *'Refactor.'* Designer: *'Mock review.'*

PM ne sab ko sun ke status doc mein likha **'On track.'** Founder ne 2 hafte baad poocha — *'feature kab launch hoga?'* — silence. Yaar, *kaam* count karna alag hai, *outcome* track karna alag.

en.title: The standup illusion
en.md:
Daily standup: API integration, bug fix, refactor, mock review. PM writes 'on track' in the status doc. Two weeks later, the founder asks when the feature ships. Silence.

Counting work is not the same as tracking outcome. A standup full of activity can sit perfectly on top of zero progress.

blocks.md:
Vague asks are the PM's daily reality. The CEO forwards an email at 11 PM: 'simple feature, just let admins export to Excel.' Sales asks for 'a Hindi version, our Tier-2 customers want it.' Support escalates 'better notifications, users keep complaining.'

None of these are scoped. All of them feel scoped. The 3-question scope test is the move that separates the PMs who get respect from the ones who get steamrolled.

For any incoming ask, you ask three questions, in order, before you write a single ticket:

1. **Who?** — which user, in which role, on which screen?
2. **What changes in their day?** — what is different, in measurable terms, after this ships?
3. **What if we do nothing?** — does the customer churn, complain, or just sigh?

If you cannot answer all three in two sentences each, you do not have a feature; you have a feeling. Send it back.

coach.name: VP-Product Vivek
coach.role: Your hands-on VP, ex-Flipkart, allergic to roadmap theatre

intro: Arre, welcome to your first week. I'm going to throw stakeholder asks at you and you tell me what kind of move it is.
Three buckets: **Translate** (it's vague but real, your job to scope it), **Sequence** (it's already scoped, decide if and when), **Push back** (it's not a product question, send it back).
Don't overthink. The wrong answer is to do all three on every ask — that's how you burn out by month four.

scenarios.situation: CEO forwards: 'Acme Corp wants a dark mode. Can we ship it next sprint? Their CTO loves it.'
scenarios.explain: Vague ask, real customer. Run the 3-question scope test. Maybe they want dark mode; maybe they want their warehouse staff to read screens at night under bad lighting. Different feature.

scenarios.situation: Engineering lead asks: 'Should we upgrade Postgres from 14 to 16 this quarter? It needs 2 weeks.'
scenarios.explain: Already scoped, technical decision with a clear cost. Your job is to weigh it against feature work and decide when, not what.

scenarios.situation: Sales says: 'Can you tell engineering to stop refactoring and ship the SSO feature faster?'
scenarios.explain: You don't tell engineering how to engineer. Translate the urgency (a deal? a deadline?) but the implementation call is theirs.

scenarios.situation: Customer success lead: 'Three customers in two weeks asked for bulk-edit on the inventory list. Should it be on the roadmap?'
scenarios.explain: Three concrete data points, identifiable feature. Your call is when, not whether to scope. The scope is already obvious.

scenarios.situation: Founder Slack at 11 PM: 'AI is the future. We need an AI strategy. Can you put together a deck for the board on Friday?'
scenarios.explain: Maximum vague. Apply the scope test before you build anything. Ask: AI for what user, doing what differently, that we can't do today? If you build the deck without scoping, you'll commit the company to a thing nobody wanted.

scenarios.situation: Designer asks: 'Do you want the modal to use rounded or square corners?'
scenarios.explain: Design's craft, not yours. Have an opinion if asked twice, but don't make it a PM decision. You're not paid to pick corner radii.

blocks.title: The classic trap: confusing 'I am busy' with 'I am useful'
blocks.md:
First-time PMs default to motion. They write tickets, run meetings, send updates, edit Confluence pages. The output looks productive. The team's actual velocity, measured by outcome, is often unchanged or worse.

The trap has a name: **the JIRA-monkey trap**. You become a high-throughput typist for everyone else's asks. You feel valuable because you're tired. You're not — you're a router, and routers do not get promoted.

The escape: every Friday, write down the **one decision** you made this week that nobody else could have made. If you can't name one, you spent the week being a router.

blocks.prompt: An engineer slacks you: 'Sales just promised the Lucknow team a Hindi UI by end of month. Is this real?' Order your moves from first to last.

items.label: Do not commit to anything in the Slack reply
items.detail: Your first move is silence. A 'sounds good!' here becomes a verbal contract by lunch.

items.label: Apply the 3-question scope test on the ask
items.detail: Who needs Hindi, on which screens, by when, and what happens if not?

items.label: Talk to the sales lead — separately, not on the engineering Slack channel
items.detail: Find out the actual customer commitment. Was it 'we'll look into it' or 'shipping in 30 days'?

items.label: Write a 1-paragraph proposal: scope, owner, date, what we drop to make room
items.detail: Now you have a position, not a panic.

items.label: Reply on the engineering Slack with the proposal and explicit tradeoffs
items.detail: Engineering finds out what's real and what's negotiable, in the same message.

hi-IN.title: Founder ne bola 'just ship it' — 14th time
hi-IN.md:
Founder Friday evening: *'Yaar, just ship it. Stop overthinking.'* PM ne ship kiya. Monday subah customers ka WhatsApp group fata. Founder bola: *'Yaar, kya scope kiya tha tumne? Itna basic miss kaise ho gaya?'*

Lesson: 'Just ship it' founder ka job hai bolna. *'Wait, scope karte hain'* PM ka job hai bolna. Dono hi job zaruri hai. Lekin agar tu sirf founder ko echo karega, tujhe rakhne ki zarurat kya hai?

en.title: When the founder says 'just ship it' for the 14th time
en.md:
Founder, Friday 6 PM: 'Just ship it, stop overthinking.' You ship. Monday 9 AM, the customer Slack is on fire. Founder, Monday 9:15: 'How did you not catch this in scoping?'

The founder's job is to push for speed. The PM's job is to push back when speed will cost more than it saves. If you only ever echo the founder, the company has no PM, just a more expensive Slack bot.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Velocity Trap
blocks.source: Anonymous APM at Skytrip, a Bengaluru-based travel SaaS (Series A, ~120 staff)
blocks.story:
On March 4, 2025, Skytrip's engineering lead pinged the new APM, Aditya, on Slack: *"We can ship a redesigned booking-confirmation page in one sprint — three engineers are unblocked. Want it?"*

Aditya, eight days into the job and desperate to look decisive, said yes. He wrote a half-page brief on Tuesday, design landed Wednesday, code merged Friday. The team shipped a beautiful new confirmation page on **March 21**. It had a nicer hero image, a clearer trip summary, and a 'share with co-traveller' button engineering had been wanting to build for months.

Three weeks of analytics later: **0.4%** of confirmed bookings used the share button. The 'nicer' confirmation page had no measurable lift on repeat-booking rate. The actual top-3 customer complaints — slow refunds, confusing baggage rules, no IRCTC fallback when flights got cancelled — were untouched.

In the post-mortem, the engineering lead said the quiet part out loud: *"We had bandwidth and a feature we wanted to build. You said go."* Aditya had optimised for **shipping** when his job was to optimise for **users not getting screwed on refunds**. The roadmap lost a sprint. The customers lost six more weeks.
blocks.takeaway: An engineering team with bandwidth is not a customer with a problem. The PM's job is to know the difference — and say no when it isn't.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Rhea's First Monday
blocks.setup:
It's **Monday, week 1** at Tarakash, a 200-person Bengaluru B2B SaaS. **Rhea** has been an APM for exactly 4 working days. At 9:47am, the CEO forwards her an email with a one-line note: *"Pls handle. Need response by EOD."*

The email is from **Mehta & Co.**, Tarakash's third-largest customer (₹38L ARR, renewal in 11 weeks). Their ops head writes: *"Your team takes 3 days to respond to support tickets. Our compliance officer needs SLA dashboards visible in the product. Please add this. Otherwise we may not renew."*

Rhea's Slack lights up. The engineering lead, Shankar, has already replied to a separate thread saying: *"We can spin up a basic SLA dashboard in 2 sprints if we cut the search-relevance work."* Rhea has 7 hours and one shot to respond.

coach.name: Director-PM Devika
coach.role: Director of Product, Tarakash · 11 years in product, allergic to feature requests dressed as ultimatums

stages.prompt: Devika DMs Rhea: *"Before you reply to anyone — what's the actual problem here?"* What do you have Rhea say back?

options.label: "The problem is Mehta wants an SLA dashboard. I'll scope it with Shankar."
options.explain: You restated the **output** as the problem. Devika sighs. The customer asked for a dashboard, but the underlying complaint is *3-day support response times*. A dashboard makes slow support **visible**, not faster. You're about to spend two sprints decorating a wound.

options.label: "The problem is our support is slow. The dashboard is their proposed fix. I want to verify the response-time number before agreeing to anything."
options.explain: **Yes.** Outcome (fast support) vs output (dashboard) cleanly separated, and you're going to check the data before you commit eng time. Devika sends back a thumbs-up and the world's smallest filter coffee emoji.

options.label: "The problem is Mehta is threatening to churn. We need to keep them happy, so let's ship the dashboard."
options.explain: Churn risk is real, but "keep customer happy" is a feeling, not a problem statement. You're about to pull two engineers off search-relevance to build a dashboard that may not move the renewal needle one millimetre. Re-read the lesson on **outcome vs output**.

options.label: "The problem is the CEO forwarded this to me, so I need to deliver something visible by EOD."
options.explain: Honest but wrong. If the only signal you optimise for is *"the CEO is watching me"*, you'll ship CEO-pleasing features for the rest of your career. Devika has seen this movie. It does not end well.

stages.prompt: Rhea pulls the support data. Median first-response time across all customers: **9 hours**. For Mehta specifically: **2.6 days** — because three of their tickets last month were tagged as 'feature request' and routed to the product backlog where they sat. What's Rhea's next move?

options.label: Reply to Mehta: "You're right, support is slow. We're shipping an SLA dashboard in 2 sprints."
options.explain: You confirmed the wrong cause. The median is fine — Mehta's specific tickets got mis-routed. A dashboard won't fix routing. You're treating an org problem with a UI bandage and burning engineers in the process.

options.label: Reply to Mehta: "The 3-day delay was a routing bug specific to your account — we're fixing the routing this week. We'll also share weekly SLA numbers in your QBR. Holding off on a dashboard until we know it's the bottleneck."
options.explain: **This is the move.** Acknowledge the pain, name the actual cause, ship the cheap fix now, and **resist the expensive fix until proven necessary**. You also bought time to validate whether a dashboard is the right answer. Devika literally claps once.

options.label: Loop in Shankar and start scoping the dashboard while also fixing the routing bug. Cover both bases.
options.explain: "Both bases" sounds responsible and is actually how PMs ship 40% more work for 5% more outcome. You haven't validated that the dashboard is needed at all. Half-credit for fixing the routing.

options.label: Forward the data to the CEO and ask what to do.
options.explain: You escalated a decision that's literally your job. The CEO forwarded this to you because they wanted **a PM to decide**. Devika notes: "If you bounce every hard call back up, you're a forwarding service, not a PM."

stages.prompt: Mehta replies, mollified but still cranky: *"Fine. But we want SLA visibility within 90 days, dashboard or otherwise."* It's now 4:30pm. How does Rhea close the loop with the CEO?

options.label: "Handled. Mehta's happy. Routing fix shipping this week."
options.explain: Too thin. The CEO doesn't know what changed, why, or what trade-off you protected. In two weeks when this comes up in a board call, the CEO has nothing to say. Half a job.

options.label: Three lines: (1) Root cause was a ticket-routing bug, not a dashboard gap. (2) Routing fix this week, weekly SLA numbers in their QBR. (3) Did NOT pull eng off search-relevance — happy to revisit in 30 days if the metric doesn't move.
options.explain: **Beautiful.** Diagnosis, action, trade-off you protected, and a built-in review date. The CEO now trusts you with the next escalation instead of micro-managing it. Devika forwards your message to the rest of the PM team as 'how to write up an escalation.'

options.label: A 600-word document with a Gantt chart, three risk scenarios, and a stakeholder map.
options.explain: The CEO will not read 600 words. You optimised for looking thorough rather than being clear. The signal-to-noise ratio of a good PM update is high. Yours is currently low.

options.label: "Resolved for now. I'll keep an eye on it."
options.explain: Vague. "Keep an eye on it" is the PM equivalent of *"we'll circle back."* The CEO has no idea whether you fixed something, dodged something, or merely promised something. Trust isn't built on vibes.

outcomes.perfect: First Monday and you didn't ship a vanity feature, didn't pull engineers off real work, and wrote an escalation summary your CEO will quote. Devika quietly bumps you up the trust ladder. **Welcome to the job, Rhea.**
outcomes.good: You avoided the worst trap (shipping the dashboard reflexively) but stumbled on either the diagnosis or the wrap-up. Re-read the **outcome vs output** section before week 2 — the next escalation is already in someone's drafts folder.
outcomes.learn: You optimised for looking responsive instead of being effective. Re-read the lesson on **what a PM is actually for** — especially the bit on customer requests being hypotheses, not specs. Good news: you have 89 more days in your first 90.

points: The PM is a translator between users, engineers, and sales/CEO — and a sequencer of finite engineering against infinite asks.
Output is what you ship; outcome is what changes for the user. Frame every initiative as an outcome before deciding the output.
The 3-question scope test (Who? What changes in their day? What if we do nothing?) separates real features from feelings.
The JIRA-monkey trap: high motion, low decisions. Every Friday, name the one decision only you could have made this week.
If you only ever echo the founder, you are not adding value — you are adding latency. Push back is part of the job description.

blocks.prompt: Think back to the last feature you saw shipped at your company (or anywhere you worked). Was it framed as an output or an outcome? If you had to retroactively write the outcome statement for it, what behavior change was supposed to happen — and did it?

lessons.title: Talking to Users Without Getting Lied To
lessons.subtitle: They tell you what they want; your job is to hear what they need

audioChapters.label: Mental model: stated want vs revealed need
Move 1 — Tell me about the last time

blocks.md:
Users will lie to you. Not maliciously — politely, helpfully, with smiles. They will say they love your product, want your dark mode, would absolutely pay for the new tier. None of it predicts what they will do.

This is a special problem in India, where saying no to a stranger is mildly impolite and saying no to a stranger who is *clearly trying their best* is socially expensive. Your interview transcripts are a museum of well-meaning lies.

The fix is not to call users liars. The fix is to **stop asking the questions that produce lies**. By the end of this lesson you will know two moves that pull real signal out of a user without making either of you uncomfortable.

blocks.title: Mental model: users tell you what they want, not what they need
blocks.md:
Treat every user statement as having two channels:

- **Channel A** — what they say. Loud, polite, optimistic, designed to make you feel good.
- **Channel B** — what they actually do, did, or are doing right now. Quiet, often invisible, always more accurate.

Good interviews tune the volume on Channel B. Bad interviews crank Channel A and call it research.

The failure mode for a junior PM is not asking the wrong questions — it's asking *future-tense* questions ('would you use…', 'would you pay for…') and treating the answers as data. They aren't. They're aspirations.

blocks.caption: Watch a single interview play twice — once with future-tense questions (loud lies), once with past-tense questions (quiet truth).

hi-IN.title: Aunty test ka satya
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. PM gaya aunty ke ghar product dikhane. Aunty ne chai pilayi, biscuit khilaye, app dekha. PM ne poocha — *'Aunty, kaisa laga? Use karoge?'*

Aunty: *'Beta, bahut acchha hai. Zaroor karungi. Mera number bhi de do, app daal ke batati hoon.'*

App install nahi hua. PM se contact bhi nahi kiya. Lekin uss 30 minute mein PM ko laga product is *fire*. **Aunty ne lie nahi kiya — Aunty ne tameez kiya.** Yeh tameez aapka roadmap fa-fa kar deti hai.

en.title: The polite no, in three acts
en.md:
You demo your product to a friend's parent. They serve you tea, listen patiently, smile, say 'this is wonderful, I'll definitely use it, send me the link.' They never install it. They never reply.

They didn't lie. They were polite. Politeness is the loudest noise in your research data, and you have to learn to filter it without becoming rude in the process.

blocks.text: Move 1 — 'Tell me about the last time…'

blocks.md:
The single most useful sentence in user research is **'Tell me about the last time you…'** It does three things at once.

First, it forces past-tense. The user can't aspire; they have to remember. Memory is messy, but messy memory is closer to truth than confident future-tense.

Second, it forces specifics. 'Tell me about the last time you exported data' produces a story with a date, a tool, a workaround, a frustration. 'Would you use an export feature' produces a polite yes.

Third, it surfaces the absence. If they cannot recall a single instance — 'umm, I don't think I have' — that is the most valuable answer in the interview. Stated demand without a single recent instance of the underlying behavior is theoretical demand. Theoretical demand does not pay for engineers.

A Mumbai fintech I consulted with was about to build a complex bill-splitter for 6 months of work. Their pre-research interview asked 'would you use a bill-splitter?' — 78 percent said yes. Their re-do, asking 'tell me about the last time you split a bill,' found that 70 percent of their target users hadn't split one in the last 90 days. Project killed. Six months saved. ₹2.4 crore not lit on fire.

blocks.title: Translating a vague 'users want X' into evidence — the 5-step interview

steps.label: Step 1 — Stop asking 'would you'
steps.body: Strike every future-tense question from your interview script. If you have 'would you use', 'would you pay', 'how often would you', delete them. They don't survive contact with reality.

steps.label: Step 2 — Replace with 'tell me about the last time'
steps.body: Convert every aspiration into a memory probe. 'Would you use an export feature?' becomes 'Tell me about the last time you needed to get data out of the dashboard.'

steps.label: Step 3 — Follow the workaround
steps.body: When they describe what they did, ask what tool they used, what was annoying, how long it took. Workarounds are revealed need with a price tag attached.

steps.label: Step 4 — Probe for absence
steps.body: If they cannot recall a single instance in the last 30-90 days, that is data, not failure. Note it. Ask 'when do you think the last time was?' and let them sit with it.

steps.label: Step 5 — Count the workarounds, not the wishes
steps.body: When you tally interviews, count specific past-tense instances of the underlying behavior. If 8 out of 10 users had a workaround in the last 30 days, you have a feature. If 8 out of 10 said 'I would use it,' you have nothing.

blocks.prompt: A user says 'I would absolutely use a Hindi UI if you built one.' What is the highest-signal next question?

choices.label: Great, what shade of saffron should the buttons be?
choices.explain: Designs the feature before validating the problem. Premature.

choices.label: Tell me about the last time the English UI actually slowed you or your team down.
choices.explain: Past-tense, specific, surfaces real pain or its absence.

choices.label: On a scale of 1 to 10, how important is Hindi UI to you?
choices.explain: Stated importance is the most consistently wrong signal in product research.

choices.label: Would your team also use it?
choices.explain: Future-tense, second-hand. Worse than the first answer, somehow.

hi-IN.title: Mummy se feedback lena
hi-IN.md:
PM ne mummy ko app dikhaya. Mummy: *'Beta, bahut sundar hai. Acchha rang hai. Tu khud bana?'* — Yeh feedback nahi hai. Yeh **gaurav** hai.

Real test: *'Mummy, Whatsapp pe pichhle hafte aapne kis aunty ko sabse zyada message kiya?'* Yeh question past-tense hai. Iska jawab actual usage data hai. Beta ka product nahi, behavior ka data.

en.title: Asking your mum is not user research
en.md:
Your mum looking at your app and saying 'beta, this is so beautiful' is not feedback. It is parental love wearing a feedback costume.

Real feedback from anyone, including your mum, comes from past-tense questions about what they actually did last week. Pride doesn't show you a churn risk; behavior does.

blocks.md:
After a user finishes their first answer, **wait three to five seconds before saying anything**. Do not nod, do not 'mm-hmm', do not move on. Just wait.

The first answer is the social-acceptable one — the one they think you want, or the one that takes the least effort to construct. The silence makes them uncomfortable enough to fill it. The second answer is closer to truth. Often it starts with 'actually…' or 'well, also…' — those are the words you came for.

This works because polite people in most cultures, and especially in India, treat silence as a conversational vacuum that has to be filled. Use it. The PMs who run the best interviews are not the ones with the cleverest questions; they are the ones who are the most comfortable with awkward pauses.

Hard mode: count to five in your head before you speak. The first time you do this, it will feel like cruelty. By the third interview, you will hear the second answer be three times more useful than the first, every time.

coach.name: VP-Product Vivek
coach.role: Your hands-on VP, ex-Flipkart, allergic to roadmap theatre

intro: Okay, you've done a few interviews. Let me read you snippets and you tell me — is this **gold** (real signal), **noise** (polite nothing), or **trap** (looks like signal, isn't)?
The question is not what they said. The question is what their answer is evidence of.
If you can't tell, default to noise. Better to lose one good signal than build a feature on a misread.

scenarios.situation: User: 'Last Tuesday I needed to send the inventory report to my boss. I exported as CSV, opened in Excel, deleted three columns, and screen-shotted it because the Excel had auto-formatted my SKU codes as dates.'
scenarios.explain: Specific date, specific workaround, specific frustration. This is exactly the past-tense, behavior-revealed signal you want.

scenarios.situation: User: 'I love your product. It's so well designed. Whoever built it really gets it.'
scenarios.explain: Compliments are not data. Note it for morale, ignore it for product decisions.

scenarios.situation: User: 'I would absolutely pay 50 percent more for an enterprise tier with SSO, audit logs, and SLA guarantees.'
scenarios.explain: Future-tense pricing answer. The 'absolutely' is doing all the lying. At launch, conversion will be a third of what they implied.

scenarios.situation: User pauses for 6 seconds, then: 'Actually... I should mention my team has been using a Google Sheet on the side because the in-app reports don't have the columns we want.'
scenarios.explain: The pause-then-actually is the silence move paying off. A side-Google-Sheet is the highest-signal artifact in B2B research.

scenarios.situation: User: 'It would be really cool if you had AI in there. Everyone's doing AI right? You should think about it.'
scenarios.explain: Trend-following without specifics. No 'last time' attached. They are repeating a headline back at you, not describing pain.

scenarios.situation: User: 'I rate it 9 out of 10. I'd recommend it to anyone in my industry.'
scenarios.explain: Stated NPS in a research call is unreliable; the user is rating the conversation, not the product. The score will tank in an actual NPS survey.

blocks.title: The classic trap: leading questions disguised as innocent ones
blocks.md:
Watch for sentences that start with **'Don't you think…?'** or **'Wouldn't it be nice if…?'** These are not questions. They are statements with a question mark stapled on. The user almost always agrees, because disagreeing is rude.

Rule of thumb: if your question implies the answer you hope for, the answer is worthless. Rewrite until the question would feel just as natural with the opposite answer.

**'Don't you find the current export confusing?'** is leading. **'Tell me about the last time you used the export'** is not. Same topic, different worlds.

blocks.prompt: You're prepping a 30-min user interview for tomorrow. Order your prep moves from first to last.

items.label: Write down the one decision this interview should help you make
items.detail: If you can't, you're collecting feelings, not running research.

items.label: Draft 5-7 past-tense questions, no future-tense, no 'would you'
items.detail: Each one starts with 'tell me about the last time' or 'walk me through how you...'

items.label: Write a 1-line opener that does NOT pitch the product
items.detail: If you pitch first, every answer becomes a polite reaction to your pitch.

items.label: Decide what 'gold signal' would look like for the decision
items.detail: Pre-commit to what evidence would change your mind. Otherwise you'll see only what confirms your plan.

items.label: Pick a notetaker (or set up a recording with consent)
items.detail: If you take notes alone, you'll miss 40 percent of the signal. Get a second pair of ears.

hi-IN.title: Demo-day dhokha
hi-IN.md:
Founder ne demo-day organize kiya. 12 prospects aaye. Sabne *'wow'* bola. Sabne business card diya. Founder ne 14 din baad email kiya. **2 reply aaye.** Reply mein bhi *'currently we're not prioritizing this, but bahut accha tha.'*

Bhai, demo-day ki *'wow'* aur usage ki *'wow'* — dono alag languages hain. Demo-day mein log free chai aur networking ke liye bhi *'wow'* bolte hain.

en.title: Why demo-day enthusiasm is a poor leading indicator
en.md:
Twelve prospects at your demo day. All said 'wow.' All gave you a card. You email them two weeks later. Two reply. Both polite passes.

Demo-day 'wow' is a social signal — they're enjoying the food and your enthusiasm. Usage 'wow' is when someone unprompted sends you a screenshot of how they used the thing. Don't confuse the two.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 30 Interviews, 4% Adoption
blocks.source: PM-2 at Khazana, a Mumbai-based personal finance app (Series B, ~3M MAU)
blocks.story:
Between **August 12 and September 9, 2024**, a PM at Khazana named Tanvi ran **31 user interviews** to validate a new 'goal-based investing' module. She had a clean script, a Calendly link, ₹500 Amazon vouchers per session, and a 38-slide synthesis deck.

The deck concluded — with charts — that **84% of interviewed users wanted goal-based investing**. The CEO loved it. Engineering scoped 11 weeks. The team shipped on **December 14, 2024**.

By **January 31, 2025**, **4.1%** of weekly actives had created a single goal. By March, that number was 3.6%, declining.

A growth analyst, bored on a Friday, re-watched five of Tanvi's recorded interviews. The pattern was brutal. Every interview opened with: *"We're thinking about building a goal-based investing feature where you can set targets like 'down payment in 5 years' — would you find that useful?"*

Of course they said yes. People at the receiving end of a free voucher and a polite question about a feature that *sounds* sensible say yes. The interviews had measured **Tanvi's enthusiasm**, not user demand. The actual top behavioural pattern in Khazana's data — users abandoning SIP setup at the bank-mandate step — was never asked about, because Tanvi had walked in with the answer.

11 engineer-weeks. ₹15,500 in vouchers. One PM who learned the hardest lesson at the highest possible price.
blocks.takeaway: If your interview question contains the answer you want, you didn't run an interview. You ran a confirmation ritual.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Rhea's Interview Script
blocks.setup:
It's **week 3** at Tarakash. Rhea has survived the Mehta escalation and earned a real assignment: figure out why **trial-to-paid conversion** has slipped from 18% to 11% over the last quarter.

She's lined up **6 user interviews** with people who started a trial in the last 30 days — 3 who converted, 3 who didn't. First call is in **45 minutes**. She drafts a script and slides it into Devika's DMs for a sanity check.

The script opens with: *"We've noticed our onboarding might be a bit confusing — would a guided tour help you get to value faster?"*

Devika reads it. Devika does not respond for 90 seconds. Then: *"Call me before that interview."*

coach.name: Director-PM Devika
coach.role: Director of Product, Tarakash · once watched a PM ask 30 leading questions in a single 25-minute call and counted them on a napkin

stages.prompt: Devika asks Rhea: *"What is wrong with the question 'would a guided tour help you?'"* What do you have Rhea answer?

options.label: "Nothing — it's a yes/no question, easy to answer, gets a clear signal."
options.explain: Devika exhales slowly. A yes/no question about a feature you describe will get **yes**, every time, from polite Indian users on a free trial. You're measuring agreeableness, not demand.

options.label: "It's a leading question — it suggests both the problem (confusing) and the solution (guided tour). I'm priming the answer."
options.explain: **Yes.** You named both the diagnosis and the solution before the user said a word. They will now spend 25 minutes politely confirming your hypothesis. Devika's blood pressure drops 4 points.

options.label: "It's a closed question — I should make it open-ended. 'Would a guided tour, a tutorial video, or a checklist help you?'"
options.explain: You added options but they're all **your** options. The user is still picking from a menu you wrote. Open-ended doesn't mean 'multiple choice in a sentence.'

options.label: "The wording is too casual — should be more formal for a B2B context."
options.explain: Tone is the least of your problems. The script is leading, hypothetical, and solution-shaped. Formality won't save it. Devika is not interested in vocabulary right now.

stages.prompt: Devika says: *"Rewrite the opener. You have 30 seconds."* Which version makes the cut?

options.label: "Walk me through the first time you logged in to Tarakash. What were you trying to do, and what happened?"
options.explain: **Clean.** Past behaviour, specific moment, no solution implied. The user will tell you what they actually did, not what they wish they'd done. This is how you find out the export button is hidden behind two clicks no one finds.

options.label: "On a scale of 1-10, how would you rate our onboarding?"
options.explain: You'll get a 7. Everyone gives a 7. Numerical ratings of vague things tell you almost nothing about what to change. "Why a 7 and not a 9" is slightly better but still in your imagination.

options.label: "What features do you wish Tarakash had?"
options.explain: Henry Ford's faster horse, but in B2B SaaS form. Users are great at describing **problems** they hit, terrible at designing **features** to fix them. You're outsourcing the PM job to the user.

options.label: "Tell me about the last time you tried to do [job-to-be-done] in Tarakash. Where did you get stuck?"
options.explain: **Even better — anchored to a specific job.** Past tense, specific event, asks about friction without naming the friction. This is what good interview craft looks like. Devika makes a small approving noise.

stages.prompt: First interview, 12 minutes in. The user (a CFO at a 40-person logistics firm) says: *"Honestly, we just couldn't figure out the integrations. We tried for 20 minutes and gave up."* Rhea's brain immediately wants to pitch the API docs upgrade she's been thinking about. **What does she do instead?**

options.label: "That's a great point — we're actually planning a major API docs upgrade. Would that have helped?"
options.explain: You jumped from listening to selling in one sentence. The user will now politely confirm your upcoming feature and you've learned **nothing new** about their actual workflow. Stay in the question for one more minute. Always.

options.label: "Tell me more about that. What were you trying to integrate, and where exactly did you get stuck?"
options.explain: **Five-and-Why's first cousin.** You stayed in curiosity, asked for the specific tool and the specific failure point. The user explains they wanted to push invoices to Tally, the docs said 'use our webhook' with no example, and they had no idea what a webhook was. Now you know the real problem isn't docs — it's a self-serve template gap.

options.label: "Got it. Anyway, moving on — next question."
options.explain: You walked past a goldmine because your script said it was time for the next question. Rigid scripts in user interviews are a way of avoiding what users are actually telling you. Half-credit only because you didn't lead.

options.label: "How many minutes was that, roughly? Were you on chrome or firefox? Mac or windows?"
options.explain: Logging environment trivia while the user is mid-confession of a real pain. You optimised for what's easy to capture, not for what matters. Devika weeps softly.

stages.prompt: After all 6 interviews, Rhea has a giant Notion doc of quotes. She has to brief Devika in the morning. **How does she synthesise?**

options.label: Count the most-mentioned features and present a top-5 list in a deck.
options.explain: Vote-counting six interviews gives you popularity, not insight. Two of those features were probably mentioned because **you asked about them**. Tally Tanvi from the Khazana field notes — that way lies a 4% adoption feature.

options.label: Group the friction moments by the **job the user was trying to do**, then look for the 2-3 jobs where multiple users got stuck at the same step.
options.explain: **This is the work.** Job → friction step → frequency. The Tally-via-webhook problem showed up in 3 of 6 interviews. That's a pattern, not a vote. Devika will let you propose a fix on this one.

options.label: Pick the most articulate quote and use it as a 'voice of customer' slide.
options.explain: One quote is an anecdote. The most articulate user is rarely the most representative one. PM theatre, not PM craft.

options.label: Send the raw Notion doc to Devika and let her draw conclusions.
options.explain: Synthesis is **your** job. Outsourcing the analysis to your boss after running the interviews defeats the purpose of running them yourself.

outcomes.perfect: You ran a real interview, not a confirmation ritual. You found a fixable bottleneck (Tally template) hiding behind a vague complaint (bad onboarding). Devika books you for a quarterly user-research review. **You're now 18 days in and already useful.**
outcomes.good: You avoided the worst leading-question traps but flinched on either the follow-up or the synthesis. Re-read the section on **5-Why's** and **job-anchored questions** — the next round of interviews is in 10 days.
outcomes.learn: You ran interviews the way Tanvi at Khazana did — with the answer pre-loaded. Re-read the lesson, especially **the difference between asking about behaviour (what did you do) and opinions (what do you think)**. Then watch one of your own recordings with the sound on. It will hurt. Do it anyway.

points: Users tell you what they want; their behavior tells you what they need. Tune for behavior, discount aspiration.
Replace every future-tense question with 'tell me about the last time…' — past tense produces stories, future tense produces fiction.
After the user's first answer, count to five before speaking. The second answer is the one you came for.
Workarounds are demand with a price tag attached; a side-built Google Sheet is the highest-signal artifact in B2B research.
If your question implies the answer you hope for, the answer is worthless. Test by flipping it — would the question feel just as natural with the opposite answer?

blocks.prompt: Recall the last user feedback you acted on (at work, in a side project, on a pitch). Was the evidence past-tense behavior or future-tense aspiration? If it was aspiration, what did the user actually do after launch — and how does that change your read on the original signal?

lessons.subtitle: A PRD is a contract with future-you, not a novel for the engineers

audioChapters.label: Mental model: PRD as contract with future-you

blocks.md:
Most PRDs fail in one of two directions. Either they are 14 pages of background, user personas, motivational quotes, and pixel mockups — and nobody reads past page 3. Or they are a one-line JIRA ticket with the word 'TBD' in 4 places, and the engineer ships exactly the wrong thing.

Neither extreme works. The fix is to think about what a PRD is *for*. Not who reads it; what it does. A PRD is the document that makes 'done' unambiguous before any code is written. If, after reading it, you and the engineer disagree on whether something is in scope, the PRD has failed regardless of how pretty it was.

This lesson teaches you to write a one-page PRD that survives, and to prioritize between PRDs without lighting your political capital on fire.

blocks.title: Mental model: a PRD is a contract with future-you
blocks.md:
When you write a PRD, the most important reader is not the engineer, the designer, or the CEO. It is **future-you**, three weeks from now, when someone asks 'wait, was this in scope?' and you have to answer without re-litigating the whole thing.

If the doc resolves the disagreement on its own, the PRD worked. If you have to rebuild the context from memory and Slack threads, the PRD failed.

This reframe changes what you write. You stop writing for an imagined audience and start writing for your own future amnesia. **Outcome, out-of-scope, done-means, risks** — those four sections protect future-you. Everything else is optional.

hi-IN.title: TBD ka tehzeeb
hi-IN.md:
PM ne PRD likha. 4 jagah likha *'TBD — to be discussed in standup.'* Standup mein discussion nahi hua. Engineer ne sprint shuru kar diya. Designer ne mock bana liya. Friday ko launch ki demo. Founder ne dekha — *'Yeh tho ekdum ulta ho gaya, scope to mera dimaag mein kuch aur tha.'*

Lesson: **TBD likhna safe nahi hai, tehzeeb hai.** Tehzeeb ka cost 4 din ka rework hai. Decide karo, ya likho 'open question, blocking — owner: PM, by Wednesday'. Lekin TBD ko PRD mein mat chhodo.

en.title: TBD is not a placeholder, it is a deferred bug
en.md:
Every 'TBD' in a PRD is a decision you've delegated to whoever notices it last. That person is usually an engineer at 4 PM on Thursday, and their interpretation will not be the one you would have chosen.

Replace TBD with one of two things: an actual decision, or 'open question, blocking, owner: PM, by Wednesday'. Both are fine. TBD is not.

blocks.md:
You will have more PRDs than engineers, always. Prioritization is not a skill — it is the *job*. Two frameworks earn their keep, not because they're cleverer than your gut, but because they make your gut auditable.

**RICE** = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort. You score each on a small scale (impact 1-5, confidence 0.5-1, reach in users-per-quarter, effort in person-weeks). The number you get is meaningless on its own; the number is meaningful when you compare it to other RICE scores. RICE works for triage of medium-sized features (a sprint to a quarter of work).

**Value vs effort 2x2** is the cheaper, faster cousin. Plot every feature on a value-axis and an effort-axis. Top-left (high value, low effort) is the obvious yes. Bottom-right (low value, high effort) is the obvious no. The interesting quadrants are top-right (high value, high effort — 'big bets', need careful timing) and bottom-left (low value, low effort — 'snacks', do them between bigger work or skip if no slack).

Neither framework decides for you. Both make your reasoning visible. The point is auditability — six months later, when the feature flopped, you can re-read your inputs and learn which one your gut was wrong about. Confidence, usually.

Bottom-left 'SNACKS — between work' blue. Bottom-right 'NO — never' grey. Five sample features plotted as dots.

blocks.title: Translating a backlog of 12 asks into a sprint plan — RICE in 5 steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Score Reach honestly
steps.body: Reach is users affected per quarter, not 'every user could theoretically use this.' If only 8 percent of admins ever open the export menu, your reach for an export feature is at most 8 percent.

steps.label: Step 2 — Score Impact on a small scale
steps.body: Use 0.25 / 0.5 / 1 / 2 / 3. Not 1-10. The narrower scale prevents 'everything is a 7' inflation. Impact 3 is reserved for things that materially shift retention or revenue.

steps.label: Step 3 — Score Confidence brutally
steps.body: 100 percent only if you have direct user evidence (interviews, instrumented behavior). 80 percent if you have indirect (sales reports, support tickets). 50 percent or lower for 'the CEO has a feeling'. Most early-stage features are 50-70 percent.

steps.label: Step 4 — Estimate Effort with engineering
steps.body: Person-weeks. Take the engineer's number and multiply by 1.5 for review, QA, and the one mid-project surprise. The 1.5x is empirical, not pessimism.

steps.label: Step 5 — Sort by score, then sanity-check
steps.body: Look at the top 5. Does the order match what your judgment says? If not, your inputs are off — usually confidence. Do not tweak the inputs to match your gut; either trust the gut and override (and write down why), or trust the inputs and override the gut. Be explicit about which you did.

blocks.prompt: Two features score within 12 percent of each other on RICE. The CEO has a strong preference for the lower-scored one. What does the framework actually tell you to do?

choices.label: Build the higher-RICE feature; data wins.
choices.explain: A 12 percent gap is within the noise of your own confidence numbers. RICE is signaling 'these are equivalent'.

choices.label: Build the CEO's choice; their gut is the tiebreaker.
choices.explain: Defaulting to HiPPO skips the actual question — what does the CEO know that your inputs missed?

choices.label: Treat the scores as equivalent and decide on a non-RICE factor: strategic fit, dependency unlock, or learning value.
choices.explain: When scores are within 15 percent, the model is signaling 'use judgment'. That's the point.

choices.label: Re-run RICE with stricter inputs until one wins.
choices.explain: Tweaking inputs to get the answer you want is how RICE becomes theatre.

hi-IN.title: Roadmap mein 'P0' ka inflation
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. PRD review meeting. Founder bola — *'yeh P0.'* VP-Sales bola — *'mera bhi P0.'* Customer success ne likha — *'humare 3 customers ke liye P0.'* Engineering manager ne calmly bola — *'Sir, agar 9 cheezein P0 hain, toh kuch bhi P0 nahi hai.'*

P0 inflation real hai. RICE ka kaam yeh nahi ki sab ko convince kare — kaam yeh hai ki dikhaye ki **9 P0 mein se 7 actually P2 hain**, with reasons.

en.title: P0 inflation in three meetings
en.md:
Roadmap meeting. The founder calls one feature P0. Sales calls another P0. Customer success calls a third P0. By Friday, nine things are P0 and the engineering manager has stopped attending.

The job of a prioritization framework is not to win the meeting. It's to make the inflation visible. RICE doesn't need to convince anyone; it just has to show that 7 of the 9 P0s are actually P2, with the reasons spelled out.

blocks.md:
Halfway through every project, you will be asked to fit more into less. Less time, less engineers, fewer designers — same scope. The default response is to compromise — half-build feature A, half-build feature B, ship a fuzzy version of both. **This is the worst possible move.**

The rule is **cut, don't compromise**. When scope must shrink, drop entire features rather than building diluted versions of every feature.

Why: a half-built feature has all the QA cost, all the documentation cost, all the support-ticket cost, and a fraction of the user value. Three features built well beat six features built halfway, every single time. Half-features become technical debt and customer complaints; cut features become future roadmap items.

The move in practice: when the engineer says 'we cannot fit all five things by Friday,' your response is 'which two of the five are we cutting completely?' — not 'which corners can we shave on each.' This will feel cruel the first time. Do it anyway.

coach.name: VP-Product Vivek
coach.role: Your hands-on VP, ex-Flipkart, allergic to roadmap theatre

intro: Cut-or-compromise time. I'll give you a mid-sprint scenario, you tell me — **cut entire feature**, **trim scope of one feature**, or **add resources / extend deadline**.
There's no universal right answer; there's a defensible answer given the situation. I'll explain the cleanest move for each.
Junior PMs default to compromise on everything. That's not a strategy, that's an avoidance pattern.

scenarios.situation: Sprint has 5 features. Engineer says 4 days behind. 1 feature (F4) is dependent on a 3rd-party API still being unstable. The other 4 are independent and on track.
scenarios.explain: Cut F4 — its dependency means it'll keep slipping anyway. Better to fully ship 4 than wobble on 5.

scenarios.situation: 1 feature (the dashboard) has 6 sub-tasks. 4 are core, 2 are 'nice to have' filters. Engineer says all 6 won't fit; 4 will.
scenarios.explain: Trim within one feature when sub-tasks are clearly tiered. Ship the 4 core, defer the 2 filters. The feature still ships intact.

scenarios.situation: Quarter has 8 features. Mid-quarter, sales close a $400K deal contingent on 1 specific feature shipping in 6 weeks instead of 12. Engineering says it's possible only if you drop 2 other features or add a contractor.
scenarios.explain: Cut 2 features. Adding a contractor mid-sprint usually slows the team in the first 3 weeks (onboarding cost). Cutting features is decisive and reversible — those features can ship next quarter.

scenarios.situation: 1 feature is 90 percent done. Last 10 percent is polish — animations, edge-case error states, accessibility audit. Engineer says 1 more week.
scenarios.explain: The last 10 percent is what the user actually feels. Extending by a week is far cheaper than the support load of an unpolished launch.

scenarios.situation: 5 features all roughly equivalent in importance. All halfway done. Engineer says only 3 will be ready Friday at full quality.
scenarios.explain: Pick 2 to cut now, ship 3 well. Compromising on all 5 means 5 half-features and 5x the support burden.

blocks.title: The classic trap: 'just one more thing' scope creep
blocks.md:
Mid-project, someone (often the founder, occasionally sales, sometimes you) realises the feature would be 'just so much better with X.' X is small. X seems harmless. X is how 4-week features become 9-week features.

The trap has a name: **the just-one-more-thing trap**. The escape: every scope addition mid-project must displace something already in scope. Not 'add to the end' — *displace*. If nothing can be displaced, the addition does not enter the sprint.

Write this in your PRD: 'Mid-sprint additions require a 1:1 displacement.' Engineers will love you. Future-you will love you more.

blocks.prompt: You're prioritizing 6 features for next quarter using value-vs-effort. Order your moves from first to last.

items.label: Define the team's quarterly outcome metric
items.detail: Without a target metric, 'value' is a vibe. Pick one number you're trying to move.

items.label: Score each feature for value (impact on the target metric, not impact in general)
items.detail: Tie value to the quarterly metric, not to a general sense of importance.

items.label: Get effort estimates from engineering, not from your gut
items.detail: Your effort estimate is wrong by 50 percent. Engineering's is wrong by 30 percent. Use theirs.

items.label: Plot all 6 on the 2x2 and identify the obvious quadrants
items.detail: Top-left does. Bottom-right doesn't. Top-right and bottom-left are the conversation.

items.label: Discuss the 'big bets' (top-right) explicitly with leadership before committing
items.detail: Big bets need timing and political cover. Don't slip them in; surface them for a yes or no.

blocks.hint: Step 1 is not 'score the features'. It's 'define what value means for this quarter'.

blocks.instruction: Write the 'Done means' section of a one-page PRD for an admin CSV export feature. Aim for 3-5 bullet points. Each bullet should be testable; an engineer should be able to point at the running feature and check yes or no.
blocks.starter:
## Done means

- Admin can click 'Export' on the inventory dashboard and download a .csv within 10 seconds for up to 50,000 rows.

blocks.expected:
## Done means

- Admin can click 'Export' on the inventory dashboard and download a .csv within 10 seconds for up to 50,000 rows.
- The CSV preserves SKU codes as text (no auto-conversion to dates by Excel) and includes the columns currently visible in the dashboard view.
- An audit log entry is created on each export, capturing user, timestamp, and row count, visible in the existing audit-log view.
- Errors over 50,000 rows return a clear message: 'Use the scheduled-export feature for larger datasets.' (no silent timeouts).

blocks.prompt: Which of these are valid reasons to cut an entire feature mid-sprint? Select all that apply.

choices.label: A blocking dependency on a 3rd-party API has become unstable
choices.explain: External instability means the feature will keep slipping; cleanest cut.

choices.label: The engineer estimating it is on holiday for 2 days
choices.explain: A 2-day absence is not a feature-level decision; that's a sprint-management adjustment.

choices.label: User research conducted mid-sprint shows the underlying problem is not real
choices.explain: If the problem isn't real, finishing the feature is a sunk-cost mistake. Cut and redeploy.

choices.label: The CEO mentioned a different priority in passing on Slack
choices.explain: Casual comments are not decisions. Confirm intent before cutting committed work.

hi-IN.title: EMI logic in product
hi-IN.md:
Compromise ka problem yeh hai ki short-term mein chhota lagta hai, long-term mein interest pile hota hai. Bilkul EMI ki tarah.

Har half-shipped feature ka monthly EMI hai — support tickets, bug reports, documentation gaps, designer ka *'iska v2 kab aayega?'* ka question. Tu yeh EMI 18 mahine bharta hai, yaa ek baar feature **cut** karke headline pain leta hai. Smart PMs cut karte hain, EMI nahi bharte.

en.title: Half-features come with EMI
en.md:
Cutting a feature is a single up-front cost — one awkward conversation. Compromising on a feature is an EMI: support tickets every week, bug reports every month, designer asking 'when's v2?' every quarter, for 18 months.

The smart PMs take the up-front cost. The exhausted ones pay EMI for years.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The PRD That Didn't Define Done
blocks.source: Engineering manager at Vahaan Logistics, a Pune-based fleet-management SaaS (Series A, ~80 staff)
blocks.story:
On **June 3, 2024**, a PM at Vahaan named Karan handed engineering a PRD titled *'Driver attendance — phase 1.'* It was 2 pages. It described the problem (fleet owners couldn't tell which drivers showed up), listed user stories ('as a fleet owner, I want to see daily attendance'), and ended with: *"Acceptance criteria: TBD with eng during sprint planning."*

Nobody filled in the TBD. Sprint planning happened on **June 7**. Engineering interpreted *'see daily attendance'* as a daily-summary table — driver name, punch-in time, status. Karan, in his head, had imagined a real-time dashboard with geo-fenced punch-in via the driver app, plus an automatic SMS to the fleet owner if more than 10% of drivers were absent.

Neither person asked. Engineering shipped the table on **June 28**. It worked beautifully.

Karan demoed it to the design partner — **Patel Transports, ₹22L ARR** — on **July 2**. The CEO of Patel looked at the table and said: *"This is just a list. Where's the SMS? Where's the map?"* Karan turned the colour of curd.

The rebuild took **2 weeks** and **3 engineers**, plus a credibility hit with Patel that took two more months to repair. The rebuilt PRD had a 'Definition of Done' section with 7 bullets, signed off by eng, design, and the design partner. It was 1 page longer than the original. It would have saved 14 days.
blocks.takeaway: If the PRD doesn't define 'done', engineering will define it for you — and they'll define it as 'whatever was easiest to build from your description.'

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Rhea's First Quarter Plan
blocks.setup:
**Week 5, Tarakash.** Rhea has earned the right to own a piece of the Q3 plan. Devika hands her the quarter brief: **2 engineers, 12 weeks, one objective — *lift trial-to-paid conversion from 11% back to 18%.*** 

Rhea has a backlog of **8 candidate features**, gathered from her interviews and the broader team:

1. **Tally integration template** (3 wks) — fixes the bottleneck she found in lesson 2.
2. **Guided onboarding tour** (2 wks) — the CEO's favourite pet idea.
3. **API docs upgrade** (5 wks) — engineering wants this badly.
4. **In-product chat support** (4 wks) — sales asked for it.
5. **Pricing page A/B test** (1 wk) — growth team's ask.
6. **SSO/Google login** (2 wks) — 4 users asked in interviews.
7. **Admin audit log** (3 wks) — Mehta from week 1 asked for this in their renewal call.
8. **Slack notification integration** (4 wks) — competitor has it.

She has roughly **24 engineer-weeks** of capacity. She has to cut to 3 features and write a defensible PRD for the lead one. Devika's calendar slot is in 90 minutes.

coach.name: Director-PM Devika
coach.role: Director of Product, Tarakash · believes a roadmap with 8 things is a wishlist with delusions

stages.prompt: Devika asks: *"What's your filter? You can't pick 3 without knowing why you're picking 3."* What does Rhea say?

options.label: "I'll pick the 3 most-requested features so we cover the most stakeholders."
options.explain: Stakeholder happiness is not the objective. The objective is **trial-to-paid 11% → 18%**. Three features that please everyone but don't move that number is how PMs ship 'busy' instead of 'effective.'

options.label: "My filter is: does this feature plausibly move trial-to-paid conversion in 12 weeks? Anything that doesn't, gets cut or deferred — even if a stakeholder asked for it."
options.explain: **Yes.** You named the objective and made it the cut-line. Now Slack notifications, audit log, and SSO are obviously off the list — they're retention/expansion features, not conversion features. Devika nods.

options.label: "I'll pick the 3 cheapest features so we can ship the most."
options.explain: Cheap features that don't move the metric are still a wasted quarter. The pricing A/B test is cheap; an audit log is cheap-ish. Neither is the bottleneck. Cost is a tiebreaker, not the criterion.

options.label: "I'll let the team vote."
options.explain: PM democracy is how you end up with the engineering team's pet feature, sales' pet feature, and the CEO's pet feature. None of which were chosen because they move the metric. Devika is now googling 'how to fire an APM.'

stages.prompt: Applying the conversion-lift filter, which **3 features** does Rhea pick?

options.label: Tally template (3w) + Guided tour (2w) + API docs (5w) = 10w. Save the rest as buffer.
options.explain: Tally and guided tour are good picks. API docs is a 5-week investment that helps **integration partners**, not trial users hitting the conversion wall. Devika points out: "Eng wants this. Eng wanting something is not the same as it moving the metric."

options.label: Tally template (3w) + Guided tour (2w) + Pricing A/B test (1w) = 6w. Pull in audit log (3w) since it helped retain Mehta.
options.explain: You started strong then added the audit log because it felt politically smart. Mehta is **renewal**, not **trial-to-paid**. You drifted off the objective in the second sentence.

options.label: Tally template (3w) + Guided tour (2w) + Pricing A/B test (1w) = 6w. Hold the remaining 18w of capacity in reserve for the 2 inevitable scope expansions and one bug-bash sprint.
options.explain: **This is mature planning.** All three picks plausibly hit conversion. You explicitly held buffer for scope creep and on-call work. Devika says: "I've been a PM for 11 years. I have never once finished a quarter at the originally-scoped capacity."

options.label: Pick all 8 — *"we'll figure out as we go."*
options.explain: 24 engineer-weeks of capacity, 24 engineer-weeks of features, zero buffer, zero scope discipline. This is the *now/now/now* roadmap from lesson 4, except it's currently lesson 3 and you're already failing the next one.

stages.prompt: Rhea picks the 3. Now she has to write the PRD for the **Tally integration template**. Which version does she ship?

options.label: A 1-pager: Problem (CFOs can't push invoices to Tally), User story ("as a CFO, I want to push invoices to Tally"), Acceptance criteria: TBD with eng.
options.explain: You re-created Karan's PRD from the field notes. Engineering will interpret 'push invoices to Tally' as 'a button that exports a CSV.' Two weeks in, you'll discover they didn't build the webhook. Re-read the field notes, then re-read them.

options.label: A 2-pager: Problem, target metric (% of trial users who complete a Tally integration in <10 mins), in-scope (one-click template, sample webhook payload, error states for top-3 failure modes), explicitly out-of-scope (Zoho, Quickbooks, custom mappings), Definition of Done (5 bullets, eng-signed).
options.explain: **Beautiful.** Problem, target metric, in-scope, **out-of-scope** (this is the bit most PMs miss), and a Definition of Done that engineering signed. You can now cut a sprint review with confidence. Devika prints this and pins it to the wall.

options.label: A 14-page document with personas, customer journey maps, competitor analysis, 4 mockups, a risk register, and an OKR alignment matrix.
options.explain: Nobody will read this. Nobody. The CEO will skim the first page, engineering will read the 'in-scope' section if you're lucky, and you'll have spent 3 days writing instead of building. PRD bloat is itself a form of avoiding the hard thinking.

options.label: A Slack thread with 4 bullet points and a Loom video.
options.explain: Will work for a 3-person startup. Will not survive contact with a 200-person org where engineering, design, support, and sales all need to find this in 6 weeks. PRDs are durable; Slack threads are not.

outcomes.perfect: You filtered ruthlessly, scoped honestly, and wrote a PRD engineering can actually build from. **Devika tells the head of eng you're 'unusually clear-eyed for someone 5 weeks in.'** You're ahead of where most APMs are at month 6.
outcomes.good: You got the filter right but stumbled on either the picks or the PRD craft. Re-read the section on **Definition of Done** and **explicit out-of-scope** — both are where rebuilds get prevented.
outcomes.learn: You optimised for breadth (lots of features, vague PRD) instead of depth (3 features, sharp PRD). Re-read the lesson, especially the parts on **the cut-line filter** and **why 'TBD with eng' is the most expensive 4 letters in product management**.

points: A PRD is a contract with future-you about what 'done' means. Outcome, out-of-scope, done-means, risks — those four sections, on one page.
TBD is not a placeholder; it is a deferred bug. Replace with a decision or a tracked open question with an owner and a date.
RICE and value-vs-effort don't decide for you; they make your reasoning auditable. When scores are within 15 percent, use judgment, not a tiebreaker.
When scope must shrink, cut entire features rather than compromising on every feature. Three things shipped well beat six things shipped halfway.
Mid-sprint additions require 1:1 displacement; if nothing can be displaced, the addition does not enter the sprint.

blocks.prompt: Look at the most recent PRD or feature spec you have written or read. Which sections protected future-you, and which were padding? If you had to rewrite it as a one-page contract — outcome, out-of-scope, done-means, risks — what would you keep, and what would you cut?

lessons.title: Roadmaps, Quarterly Plans, and Saying No
lessons.subtitle: A roadmap is a story you tell to align, not a contract you sign in blood

audioChapters.label: Mental model: roadmap as story, not contract

blocks.md:
Most PMs build roadmaps the way they were taught — Gantt charts with feature names lined up against months, color-coded, beautiful, and almost entirely fictional by week six. The Gantt chart is not the problem; the *expectation* the Gantt chart sets is the problem.

**A roadmap that's longer than a quarter is fiction.** Not because PMs are bad, but because the inputs change faster than the planning cycle: customers behave differently, competitors move, engineering finds the schema is wrong, the founder reads a tweet. By month four, half the roadmap is irrelevant. The team learns to treat roadmaps as a thing you nod at and ignore.

This lesson teaches you to build a roadmap that tells a coherent story without overpromising, and to say no to off-roadmap asks without losing the deal or the relationship.

blocks.title: Mental model: a roadmap is a story you tell to align, not a contract you sign
blocks.md:
A roadmap has one job: get sales, engineering, design, customer success, and the board to all describe the next 90 days the same way. That's it. Same story, told confidently, in three different rooms.

It is **not** a contract. The customer who waves your roadmap at you in renewal asking 'where is feature X you promised in October?' has misunderstood what they were given. Your job is to set the expectation, in the doc itself, that direction is firm and dates are not.

If you remember nothing else from this lesson, remember: **commit to direction, not to dates beyond the current quarter**. Direction is auditable in 6 months ('did you build broadly the things you said you would?'). Dates are not survivable past 90 days.

hi-IN.title: Roadmap aur shaadi-card
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Roadmap aur shaadi-card mein bahut similarity hai. Dono pe specific date likhi hai. Dono ko log frame karke rakhte hain. Aur dono mein **schedule reality se 70 percent match karta hai, baaki 30 percent improvise** hai.

Lekin shaadi-card pe likha tha *'7 PM sharp'*. 7 PM mein dulha bhi nahi tha, dulhan bhi nahi thi, photographer bhi nahi tha. Sab 9 baje pohche. Shaadi 11 baje shuru hui. **Card galat nahi tha, expectation galat tha.**

Roadmap ka bhi yahi haal hai. Date mat dekho — direction dekho.

en.title: Why the wedding card is a useful metaphor for roadmaps
en.md:
An Indian wedding card says 'ceremony at 7 PM sharp.' The ceremony starts at 11. Nobody is angry; everyone understood the card was an aspiration, not a contract. The card was never wrong; the expectation it set, by being specific, was wrong.

A roadmap with calendar dates beyond the current quarter is a wedding card. The doc is fine; the expectation it sets is the problem. State, on the doc, what is firm (direction) and what is aspirational (dates).

blocks.md:
The strongest roadmap format for most teams is **three columns: NOW, NEXT, LATER**. Replace your Gantt with this and watch your stakeholder conversations get 30 percent shorter.

**NOW** is what's in flight this sprint or this 4-6 week chunk. Everything in NOW has a PRD, an engineering owner, and an estimated ship window. NOW is the most committed column; if something is here, you have a contract with the team to ship it.

**NEXT** is what's queued for this quarter, scoped enough that you could start within 2 weeks if NOW finishes early. NEXT items have a one-page PRD and a rough effort estimate, but no calendar date. NEXT is firm in priority order, soft in timing.

**LATER** is everything else worth talking about — direction-setting, big bets, the things you want stakeholders to know are in your peripheral vision. LATER items might never ship; that's fine. The promise is 'these are the directions we're tracking,' not 'these will be built.' Be explicit about that in the doc.

A Bengaluru SaaS at 50 employees switched from quarterly Gantt to now/next/later in early 2026. Roadmap-related Slack noise dropped by 60 percent. Sales stopped pre-selling unbuilt features. Engineering stopped seeing the roadmap as a threat. Same set of features, same team, just a different framing.

blocks.title: Translating a 22-item backlog into a now/next/later roadmap — 5 steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Force a quarterly outcome
steps.body: Pick the one metric the team is moving this quarter. Activation? Retention? ARR? Without this, NOW becomes 'whatever feels urgent' and NEXT becomes a wishlist.

steps.label: Step 2 — Drop everything that doesn't map to the outcome
steps.body: If a feature doesn't plausibly move the quarterly metric, it does not belong in NOW or NEXT. It can live in LATER as a direction signal, or in your private backlog.

steps.label: Step 3 — Cap NOW at 2-3 items
steps.body: More than 3 in-flight items per pod and you lose focus. If everything is NOW, nothing is NOW. The cap forces you to sequence.

steps.label: Step 4 — Sequence NEXT in priority order, no dates
steps.body: 5-6 items maximum. Numbered 1, 2, 3 in priority. Stakeholders can argue the order; they cannot extract a date.

steps.label: Step 5 — Make LATER a story, not a list
steps.body: Group LATER items by theme: 'expand internationally', 'enterprise readiness', 'mobile experience'. Themes survive when individual features drop. Lists die feature by feature.

blocks.prompt: Why does a now/next/later roadmap reduce stakeholder noise compared to a Gantt chart?

choices.label: It hides information from stakeholders
choices.explain: It hides nothing — it just labels the commitment level of each item.

choices.label: It explicitly labels which items are committed and which are directional, so arguments happen at the right level of certainty
choices.explain: Stakeholders argue NOW scope, NEXT order, LATER themes — three different conversations, none of them about extracting a calendar date.

choices.label: It's shorter, so people read less
choices.explain: Shorter helps but isn't the structural reason.

choices.label: It removes engineering's input
choices.explain: Engineering's input is more visible, not less, in this format.

hi-IN.title: Investor update mein roadmap dikhana
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Founder ne investor update mein 8-feature ka colorful roadmap chipka diya. Investor ne 90 din baad poocha — *'feature 6 kab aa raha hai? October mein dikhaya tha.'*

Founder ne PM ko Slack kiya 11 PM ko: *'why is feature 6 not done? You committed in the deck.'* PM ne reply kiya: *'Sir, woh deck mein **direction** thi, **commitment** nahi.'*

Lesson: investor decks mein bhi **commit nahi karte 90 din se aage**. Direction dikhao, dates mat. Investor smart hain — roadmap fiction unhone bhi padha hai.

en.title: Investor decks are a roadmap trap
en.md:
Founders love putting an 8-feature, color-coded roadmap into the investor deck. Investors then quote it back to you, 90 days later, asking where feature 6 is.

The fix: in any external doc, label what is committed (this quarter, with effort estimates) and what is directional (themes you're tracking). Investors with operating experience will respect the distinction. The ones who insist on dates have probably never built a product.

blocks.md:
Sales will ask you to commit a feature to close a deal. A founder will ask you to add 'just one thing' to the sprint. A customer success lead will ask you to fix a bug for a specific account by Tuesday. You cannot say yes to all of them; you also cannot say no like a wall.

The **polite no template** is the move that lets you turn down off-roadmap asks without burning the relationship:

> *'Help me understand: what's the deal size, what's the timing, and which 5 other customers want this? I'll come back tomorrow with a yes, a no, or a swap.'*

Three things this does. First, it does not refuse — it asks for information. Asking is not refusing; nobody can be angry at being asked. Second, it surfaces evidence — sales will either bring real numbers (in which case you'll often say yes) or fold (in which case you've protected the roadmap without saying no). Third, it offers a swap — you're not adding work, you're trading. Engineering capacity is conserved.

Most asks die at step 1. Sales doesn't have the data. Customer success doesn't have 5 other accounts. The founder's 'just one thing' is actually a hunch from a podcast. Your work is done; the asker walks away with their dignity intact and a clear next step. You walk away with your sprint.

intro: Off-roadmap asks. I'll throw scenarios; you tell me — **yes (real swap)**, **polite no via 3 questions**, or **escalate (above your pay grade)**.
There is no universal yes-no rule. There is only 'do you have the data and authority to decide here, or not.'
If you escalate everything, you're a router. If you say no to everything, you're a wall. Both lose you the team.

scenarios.situation: Sales lead: 'Acme Corp wants SSO by next month or they walk. ₹38L renewal. Renewal in 6 weeks.'
scenarios.explain: Concrete data, big deal, fits the team's enterprise theme. Yes, with a swap — propose what gets pushed from NEXT to make room.

scenarios.situation: Sales lead: 'I have a feeling our prospects would close faster if we had a public roadmap page.'
scenarios.explain: Run the 3 questions. 'How many deals stalled because of no public roadmap? Which prospects asked? What did they say?' If they have answers, reconsider; usually they don't.

scenarios.situation: Founder DMs: 'Saw a YouTube video about AI agents. We need an AI strategy by Friday for the board.'
scenarios.explain: Strategic scope question above sprint-level. Don't say no to a founder strategy ask alone; escalate via your manager so the answer is co-owned.

scenarios.situation: Customer success: '3 enterprise customers in 2 weeks asked about audit logs for compliance. Renewals stacked over the next quarter.'
scenarios.explain: Convergent signal across multiple accounts, clear theme (enterprise readiness), measurable cost-of-inaction. Yes, surface it as a NEXT candidate.

scenarios.situation: Founder: 'Our competitor just launched a Slack integration. Can we ship one by end of month?'
scenarios.explain: Reactive ask without user evidence. Run the 3 Qs: how many of OUR customers asked, what would they actually do with it, what does it displace? Often the competitor's launch is a vanity move that won't move metrics.

scenarios.situation: Sales: 'Can we offer a custom integration to Brand X for ₹4L one-time? They want it in 2 weeks.'
scenarios.explain: Custom one-off integrations are a strategic pricing/architecture decision (services revenue vs product roadmap). Escalate; this isn't a sprint-level call.

blocks.title: The classic trap: turning your roadmap into a backlog
blocks.md:
When stakeholders push, the path of least resistance is to add their ask to LATER and say 'it's on the roadmap'. Within three months your LATER column has 47 items, the roadmap looks impressive, and you've quietly committed to nothing.

The trap has a name: **the roadmap-as-graveyard trap**. Items go in, they don't come out. Stakeholders eventually realise the roadmap is theatre.

The escape: cap LATER at 8-10 items, organised by 3-4 themes. Anything that doesn't fit a theme either becomes one (with reasoning) or is declined. 'On the roadmap' should mean something. Otherwise it means nothing.

blocks.prompt: Which of these are valid uses of a roadmap? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Telling sales, engineering, and the board the same coherent story for the next 90 days
choices.explain: Alignment is the primary job. One story, three audiences.

choices.label: Committing to a customer that feature X will ship by month Y
choices.explain: That's a contract, not a roadmap. Roadmaps don't bind to specific dates beyond the current quarter.

choices.label: Making the *why* behind sequencing visible — not just the *what*
choices.explain: If a roadmap is just a list of features, you've built a backlog. Roadmaps explain the order.

choices.label: Listing every JIRA ticket for the next 12 months
