hi-IN.title: Yes-bhai PM ka anjaam
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Ek PM tha — sabko *'haan, kar dete hain'* bolta tha. Sales ko haan, founder ko haan, customer success ko haan. Sab khush.

3 mahine baad: 47 items NEXT mein, 19 items 'this quarter' mein, 8 features mid-build, kuch bhi shipped nahi. Founder ne 1:1 mein bola: *'yaar tumhe hum saying yes ke liye hire nahi kiya. Tumhe **decide** karne ke liye hire kiya.'*

Yes-bhai PMs first 3 mahine mein team ke favorite hote hain. 6 mahine mein sab ka bharosa kho dete hain.

en.title: The Yes-PM career arc
en.md:
Yes-PMs are popular for the first 90 days. Sales loves them, the founder loves them, customer success thinks they finally found a partner.

By day 180, the team realises nothing has shipped, the roadmap is a wishlist, and the Yes-PM has been promising the same three quarters' worth of work to four different stakeholders. The trust they built saying yes is destroyed in one missed quarter.

The job is to decide, not to please. Saying no is not optional; it is the deliverable.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Now/Now/Now Roadmap
blocks.source: Group PM at Sahara Edu, a Gurgaon-based K-12 ed-tech (Series C, ~450 staff)
blocks.story:
On **April 8, 2024**, Sahara's product org adopted a 'now/next/later' roadmap framework after reading a popular Medium post. The Q2 plan had **6 things in 'now', 9 in 'next', 12 in 'later'**. Beautiful. Colour-coded. Linked to OKRs. The CPO showed it at the all-hands.

By **May 6**, two of the 'next' items had been pulled into 'now' because *"the customer demoed and really wants it."* By **June 11**, four more had been pulled in. By **end of Q2**, 'now' contained **14 items** and 'next' contained 1. Nothing was 'later' anymore — they had all become 'now-but-quieter.'

Nobody had cut anything. The roadmap had become a wishlist with a colour scheme.

The team shipped **8 of the 14**. Two shipped late and broken. Four shipped on time but were thinner than promised. The remaining six slipped to Q3, where the same pattern repeated.

By **September 2024**, the on-call rotation had **4 engineers on stress leave** in a 22-person team. The two senior PMs had quit citing 'roadmap whiplash.' Sahara's NPS dropped from 42 to 19 over six months because *every single feature shipped felt half-baked.*

In the **January 2025** post-mortem, the new VP-Product wrote one line at the top of the doc: *"A roadmap that doesn't say no isn't a roadmap. It's a hostage list."*
blocks.takeaway: 'Now/next/later' isn't a framework. It's a discipline. If everything keeps becoming 'now', you've adopted the colour scheme without the discipline.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Rhea's Q3 Polite-No
blocks.setup:
**Week 8, Tarakash.** Rhea's Q3 plan is locked: Tally template, guided tour, pricing A/B test. 6 weeks of work, 18 weeks of buffer, all aimed at the trial-to-paid metric.

**It is Tuesday, 11:14am.** The CEO walks into Rhea's standup, smiles at the team, and says: *"Quick one. I had a great call with Aanya from BigBank Capital last night. They're considering us for a 50-seat pilot. They need: (1) SAML SSO, (2) custom branding, (3) a usage-based billing add-on, (4) audit log exports, (5) an EU data-residency option. Can we get all 5 in Q3?"*

The team looks at Rhea. Engineering lead Shankar's left eye is twitching. The CEO is still smiling. Rhea has to respond now, on her feet, in front of seven people.

coach.name: Director-PM Devika
coach.role: Director of Product, Tarakash · has said no to 14 CEOs across 3 companies and is still alive

stages.prompt: What does Rhea say in the room, **right now**?

options.label: "Yes! Let's do it. We'll figure out a way."
options.explain: You just committed your team to ~22 weeks of work in a 12-week quarter, in front of witnesses, and abandoned the conversion-lift objective. Shankar's twitch is now seismic. Devika, watching on Slack, types and deletes three messages.

options.label: "Great prospect. Before I say yes or no, can I take 24 hours to map this against our Q3 plan and come back with a real answer?"
options.explain: **This is the right answer in the room.** You acknowledged the opportunity, did not commit, and bought time to think. CEO nods — they don't actually want a yes-person, they want a thoughtful answer. Devika sends you a single sparkles emoji.

options.label: "No, our quarter is locked. We can revisit in Q4."
options.explain: Correct intuition, brutally wrong delivery. The CEO loses face in front of the team and now thinks you're rigid. There's a difference between *saying no* and *saying it as your first sentence with no diagnosis*. Half-credit for the spine.

options.label: "That's a Shankar question — Shankar, what do you think?"
options.explain: You threw the engineering lead under the bus to dodge the call. Shankar will not forget. Trade-off decisions are PM work — that's literally why the role exists. Devika is now drafting a quietly disappointed Slack message.

stages.prompt: It's now Wednesday morning. Rhea has 22 hours to write the trade-off memo. What's the **structure**?

options.label: A long apologetic note explaining why we can't do it.
options.explain: Apologies are not a framework. The CEO doesn't want feelings, they want a thinking artifact they can take to BigBank. You'll lose the room.

options.label: (1) The opportunity (BigBank pilot, $X ARR potential). (2) The cost (5 features, ~22 eng-weeks). (3) Current Q3 plan and what we'd cut to fit. (4) Three options: A) full yes (cut Q3 plan), B) partial yes (SSO + audit log only, ~5 wks), C) full no with a Q4 commitment. (5) Recommendation + why.
options.explain: **Textbook.** Opportunity, cost, current commitment, **3 named options with explicit trade-offs**, your recommendation. The CEO can now make an informed decision instead of reacting. Devika forwards this to the rest of the PM team as 'how to write a trade-off memo.'

options.label: A spreadsheet listing every feature, its cost, and a colour-coded RAG status.
options.explain: Spreadsheets are great for capacity planning. They are not great for forcing a CEO to make a decision. You handed over data without a recommendation, and the CEO will pick the most ambitious row.

options.label: Just SSO and audit log — they're cheapest, hide the rest.
options.explain: You unilaterally re-scoped the deal without showing the CEO the trade-off. When BigBank asks about EU data residency in week 6, the CEO discovers what you cut from someone else. Career-limiting move.

stages.prompt: In the memo's **'Option B (partial yes)'** section, Rhea picks SSO + audit log. **Why those two?**

options.label: "They're the smallest features."
options.explain: Cheapness is a tiebreaker, not a reason. The CEO will ask: *"why these two and not the others?"* and "they were cheap" is not a satisfying answer.

options.label: "SSO + audit log are also asks from existing customers (Mehta, 2 others) — building them serves enterprise readiness more broadly, not just BigBank. Custom branding, usage billing, EU residency are BigBank-specific bets that we shouldn't take until BigBank signs."
options.explain: **This is the move.** You separated **horizontal bets** (SSO, audit — useful to many) from **vertical bets** (branding, billing, EU — useful to one prospect). The horizontal bets are worth doing pre-signature; the vertical bets aren't. Devika could not have framed it better.

options.label: "Engineering said they were the easiest."
options.explain: Engineering opinion is input, not strategy. Also: 'easy' for whom? An audit log is *easy* until you discover the audit needs to be tamper-proof and now it's a 6-week project.

options.label: "Random — both seemed reasonable."
options.explain: If you can't defend the picks, you can't defend the cuts. The PM job is largely the art of being able to explain *why this and not that*.

stages.prompt: The CEO reads the memo and replies: *"Let's go with Option B. Tell BigBank we'll do SSO and audit in Q3, the rest in Q4 if they sign."* How does Rhea **lock in** the trade-off so it doesn't quietly drift back to Option A?

options.label: "Great, will inform the team." Update the Notion roadmap.
options.explain: Updating Notion isn't a commitment, it's a colour change. In 3 weeks the CEO will forget Option B was the deal and ask why custom branding isn't ready. You haven't built any guard rails.

options.label: (1) Reply with explicit confirmation of what was cut from Q3 to make room (the pricing A/B test, deferred to Q4). (2) Send a 4-line summary to the BigBank thread so the deal is anchored. (3) Update the Q3 plan doc with a new line: *"Rev-1, May 7: added SSO+audit, deferred pricing A/B per CEO call."*
options.explain: **Three lines of defence.** The cut is named, the customer expectation is anchored, and the change has a versioned trail. In week 9 when someone asks why the pricing A/B isn't shipping, you have the receipts. Devika is now actively recommending you for full PM promotion.

options.label: Add the 2 features to Q3 and quietly hope nobody notices the pricing A/B is still on the plan too.
options.explain: Hope is not a strategy. This is exactly the Sahara Edu pattern from the field notes — features get added, nothing gets cut, and 6 months later the team is on stress leave.

options.label: Tell Shankar to figure out how to fit it in.
options.explain: You delegated the trade-off decision to engineering, which is the opposite of the PM job. Also Shankar will absorb it by working the team weekends, and you've just bought a quiet attrition problem.

outcomes.perfect: You handled the CEO ambush, wrote a memo your CEO can actually decide from, and locked the trade-off so it survives the next 12 weeks. **Devika tells you privately: 'You just did the hardest thing in the job. Most PMs never learn it.'** Q3 stays on track.
outcomes.good: You bought time and wrote a reasonable memo, but stumbled on either the option-design or the lock-in. Re-read the section on **horizontal vs vertical bets** and **versioning your roadmap changes**. Both will save you in Q4.
outcomes.learn: You either said yes to everything or said no without a plan. Re-read the lesson, especially **the polite-no template** and the Sahara Edu field notes. The roadmap that says yes to everything is the roadmap that ships nothing well.

points: A roadmap is a story you tell to align, not a contract you sign. Commit to direction; don't commit to dates beyond the current quarter.
Use NOW / NEXT / LATER columns: NOW is committed with ship dates, NEXT is scoped and prioritized without dates, LATER is themed direction.
Cap NOW at 2-3 items per pod; cap LATER at 8-10 items grouped by 3-4 themes. Without a cap, the roadmap becomes a graveyard.
The polite no template: 'Help me understand — deal size, timing, who else wants it? I'll come back tomorrow with yes, no, or swap.' Most asks die at step 1.
The Yes-PM is popular for 90 days and useless by day 180. Saying no with reasons is not optional; it is the deliverable.

lessons.subtitle: Ship-day is the start of the work, not the finish line

audioChapters.label: Mental model: ship-day is day 0, not day 30

blocks.md:
Most teams treat the launch blog as the finish line. The team writes a Slack post, the founder tweets a thread, and everyone moves on. Three weeks later, when someone asks 'how is the new feature doing?' the answer is a vague 'well, I think.' Sometimes it's worse — silence.

This is the most expensive habit in early-stage product. You shipped the feature. The next 30 days tell you whether the feature should be promoted, fixed, or quietly killed. If you don't run that loop, every feature you ship is a coin flip you weren't allowed to look at.

By the end of this lesson you will know how to anticipate launch failures *before* they happen, and how to read post-launch data with enough rigor to actually decide what to do next.

blocks.title: Mental model: ship-day is day 0, not day 30
blocks.md:
Reframe a launch as the **start** of the data-collection phase, not the end of the work phase. The build phase ends on ship-day; the learning phase begins.

Until you've watched 30 days of post-launch behavior, the feature has not actually shipped — only the code has. The product question — *did this work?* — is open. Open questions deserve attention. Closed-by-default-after-ship-day is how teams ship 47 features in a year and don't know which ones helped.

If you are honest with yourself, you will probably kill 20 percent of the features you ship within 90 days. That is not failure — that is the system working. The failure mode is not killing them, leaving them in the product, and accruing 18 months of support cost on a feature that's actively hurting retention.

hi-IN.title: Launch-day fanfare ka satya
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Launch-day pe LinkedIn pe 4 posts. Founder ne thread chalaya. PM ne *'we're so excited'* likha. Designer ne case study post kiya. Engineering manager ne quote-tweet kiya.

21 din baad: feature ka usage 3 percent. Slack pe koi mention nahi. PM ko poocha — *'kaisa chal raha hai?'* — *'haan, traction aa raha hai dheere dheere.'* Yeh translation hai *'mujhe pata nahi'* ka.

**Launch fanfare se traction predict nahi hota. Day-30 cohort retention se hota hai.**

en.title: Why LinkedIn launch theatre is the worst leading indicator
en.md:
On launch day, four people post about it on LinkedIn. The founder threads. Engineering quote-tweets. By week three, the feature has 3 percent adoption and nobody mentions it.

Launch fanfare predicts nothing about traction. The only signals that matter are activation rate (day 1-7), retention of users who tried the feature vs those who didn't (day 14-30), and support ticket themes (day 0-30). Everything else is theatre.

blocks.md:
A **pre-mortem** is a 30-minute team exercise, run 1-2 weeks before launch, where you imagine the launch has failed catastrophically and you list every reason why. The frame is past-tense: *'It is now 30 days post-launch. The feature has flopped. Why?'*

This works because forcing a past-tense failure frame breaks the optimism that surrounds late-stage projects. Teams who say 'what could go wrong?' produce 4-5 risks. Teams who say 'imagine it has already gone wrong; tell me the story' produce 15-20 risks, ranked by likelihood. The same brains, two different prompts, very different output.

A Bengaluru SaaS shipping a billing redesign ran a pre-mortem on a Tuesday in March 2026. The team produced 17 failure modes; 4 were mitigated immediately, 6 led to a 1-week launch delay (worth it), 7 were accepted as risks-to-watch. After launch, 5 of the 17 actually happened — but all 5 were on the list, monitored, and addressed within 48 hours. Compare to their previous launch, where they did no pre-mortem and spent 3 weeks fighting a fire that they could have caught in the room.

The move is simple: run the meeting. The cost is 30 minutes. The skip is the most common form of false economy in product.

blocks.title: Translating a pre-mortem into a launch-readiness plan — 5 steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Schedule the meeting 1-2 weeks pre-launch
steps.body: Late enough that the feature is real, early enough that you can act on findings. 30 minutes, all 4-6 people involved (PM, eng, design, CS, QA, maybe sales).

steps.label: Step 2 — Set the past-tense frame
steps.body: 'It is 30 days after launch. The feature has flopped. Tell me the story of why.' Insist on past-tense. People will slip; gently correct them.

steps.label: Step 3 — Brainstorm silently for 5 minutes
steps.body: Silent first, talking second. Otherwise the loudest voice anchors the room. Each person writes their failure modes on stickies or in a doc, no discussion.

steps.label: Step 4 — Group, prioritize, classify
steps.body: Group similar items. For each, the team votes: high / medium / low likelihood, and high / medium / low impact. Top quadrant (high likelihood, high impact) goes to 'mitigate now'. Most others go to 'accept + monitor'.

steps.label: Step 5 — Convert mitigations to owners and dates; convert monitors to dashboard items
steps.body: Every 'mitigate' item gets a name and a date before the meeting ends. Every 'monitor' item gets a metric name and a target threshold for action. Walk out with a plan, not a list of fears.

blocks.prompt: Why does the past-tense framing ('imagine it has already failed') produce more risks than the future-tense framing ('what could go wrong')?

choices.label: It triggers loss-aversion in the team.
choices.explain: Indirectly true, but not the structural reason.

choices.label: Past-tense forces explanation; the brain has to construct a causal story, which surfaces specific mechanisms.
choices.explain: 'It failed because…' demands a why. 'What could go wrong' is open and the optimistic brain answers 'probably not much'.

choices.label: It's funnier, so people engage more.
choices.explain: Pre-mortems are not noticeably more fun.

choices.label: It removes the project lead's bias.
choices.explain: It reduces optimism bias broadly, but not specifically the project lead's.

hi-IN.title: Pre-mortem Vs. PM ka jugaad
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. PM ne pre-mortem skip kiya. *'Yaar, time nahi hai, sab smart log hain, sambhal lenge.'*

Launch ke 9 din baad: support ticket flood. CSV Excel mein khul nahi raha kyunki SKU codes date ban gaye. Customer Slack pe complaints. PM ne 2 din me hot-fix shipped kiya. Founder ne 1:1 mein bola: *'yaar, yeh humein launch se 1 hafta pehle kyu nahi pata laga?'*

30 minute meeting ne 5 din ka rework save kiya hota. **Pre-mortem ka cost shaadi ke buffet ke barabar hai. Skip ka cost shaadi cancel ke barabar hai.**

en.title: The cost of skipping a pre-mortem
en.md:
Skipping a pre-mortem feels efficient. 30 minutes saved, on a team that is already busy. The implicit logic: 'we're smart, we'll catch the issues as they come.'

The issues come, on day 9, as a Slack flood from customers. The fix takes 2 days. The trust takes 4 weeks to recover. A 30-minute meeting would have caught 12 of the 14 issues that turned up. Pre-mortems are the highest-ROI meeting in product. Schedule them.

blocks.md:
After launch, run a tight loop for the first 7 days, then a slower loop through day 30. The 7-day window is where you catch fires; the 30-day window is where you decide whether to double down, fix, or kill.

**Day 0-1**: error rate, support ticket volume. Anything red, hot-fix immediately. Goal: zero customer-facing fires by end of day 1.

**Day 2-7**: activation rate (% of eligible users who tried the feature) and find rate (% who got to it). If activation is below 30 percent in a B2B context, the feature is hard to find. That's a positioning problem, not a product one — fix the in-app prompt before fixing the feature.

**Day 7-14**: week-1 retention of users who tried the feature vs those who didn't. If users who tried it have **lower** retention than users who didn't, you have a feature that's actively hurting; investigate before you spend on adoption.

**Day 14-30**: day-30 retention, support ticket themes (not just count — patterns), and the answer to the original outcome question. Did the metric you committed to in the PRD move?

Write the answer down on day 30. Three sentences. Share it with the team. This is the **post-launch debrief** — and the PMs who do this consistently get promoted within 18 months. The PMs who don't keep shipping coin flips.

coach.name: VP-Product Vivek
coach.role: Your hands-on VP, ex-Flipkart, allergic to roadmap theatre

intro: Post-launch reads. I'll give you 6 mid-launch data points. You tell me — **promote** (the feature is working, push adoption), **fix** (real signal of a real problem, fix before promoting), or **kill** (cut losses, write the postmortem).
There is no universal threshold; there is what the data is telling you, and what your judgment says about cost-of-doing-nothing.
Don't kill on day 3. Don't promote on day 30 without checking retention. Both are common mistakes.

scenarios.situation: Day 14: activation 62%, day-7 retention of users who tried it is 8 percentage points HIGHER than non-users, support tickets show 3 minor UX nits.
scenarios.explain: Strong activation, positive retention delta, only minor issues. Push adoption — in-app prompt, sales enablement, blog post.

scenarios.situation: Day 7: activation 18%, find rate 22% (people aren't getting to the feature), retention can't be measured yet.
scenarios.explain: Activation is low because find rate is low — a positioning problem. Fix the in-app prompt or onboarding before judging the feature itself.

scenarios.situation: Day 21: activation 55%, day-14 retention of users who tried it is 11 percentage points LOWER than non-users.
scenarios.explain: Negative retention delta is a stop signal — but at 21 days, you usually investigate before killing. Find out which subgroup is leaving and why; might be a fixable subset.

scenarios.situation: Day 30: outcome metric (time-to-first-invoice) hasn't moved at all. Activation is healthy at 48%. Users are using the feature but the outcome it was supposed to drive is unchanged.
scenarios.explain: The feature works but doesn't drive the outcome you committed to. That's the cleanest kill signal — engagement without value. Write the postmortem and reclaim the engineering capacity.

scenarios.situation: Day 5: zero customer-facing errors, activation 35%, but 14 support tickets all asking 'how do I undo this?' — there's no undo button.
scenarios.explain: Theme in support tickets is a clear product gap. Fix the undo before promoting the feature; otherwise every new user generates a support ticket.

scenarios.situation: Day 30: outcome metric moved 4% (against a 12% target). Retention delta is +2 percentage points. Mixed.
scenarios.explain: Partial signal in the right direction but short of target. Investigate which user segments saw the most lift, double down on those, decide on the rest. Don't kill prematurely; don't promote before tightening.

blocks.title: The classic trap: vanity metrics on launch day
blocks.md:
On launch day, the easiest numbers to share are the largest ones. Page views on the launch blog. Tweet impressions. Total sign-ups in the launch window. PR mentions.

These are **vanity metrics** — they go up with marketing effort, not with product success. They are uncorrelated with whether the feature did its job.

The trap has a name: **the launch-blog illusion**. The escape: agree, before launch, on the 3-4 metrics you'll judge the feature by *at day 30*. Write them in the PRD. Ignore everything else on launch day. The team that fixates on launch-day vanity ships features no user uses, then fixates on the next launch.

blocks.prompt: You're 7 days post-launch and the data is mixed. Order your moves to decide what to do next.

items.label: Pull the 4 metrics agreed in the PRD: activation, find rate, retention delta, outcome metric
items.detail: Stick to what you committed to. Don't shop for metrics that confirm a story.

items.label: Look at activation and find rate first — these tell you if the feature is even discoverable
items.detail: If find rate is low, nothing else can be evaluated. Fix discovery before judging the feature.

items.label: Read the support ticket themes from the last 7 days
items.detail: Themes (not counts) tell you what's specifically broken. 12 tickets about one thing is signal; 12 random tickets is noise.

items.label: Check retention delta vs the control cohort
items.detail: Are users who tried the feature better-retained, neutral, or worse? Worse is a stop signal.

items.label: Decide: promote / fix / kill, and write 3 sentences explaining why
items.detail: The 3-sentence verdict forces clarity. If you can't write it, you don't have a decision yet.

blocks.hint: First look at discovery, then at value. Don't judge the feature until you know users found it.

blocks.instruction: You shipped a 'bulk-edit' feature 14 days ago. Activation is 41% (target was 35%). Day-7 retention of users who tried it is 6pp HIGHER than non-users. Outcome metric (time spent on inventory updates) is down 22% (target was 15%). Write the 3-sentence post-launch verdict you would share with the team.
blocks.expected:
## Bulk-edit: 14-day verdict

The feature is working: activation cleared the 35% target by 6 points, day-7 retention is 6pp better for users who tried it, and time-on-inventory-updates is down 22% (well past our 15% goal). Strongest evidence so far is the retention delta, which suggests bulk-edit is becoming a sticky habit rather than a one-time novelty. Recommend we promote in-app, brief sales by Friday, and do a 30-day re-check before adding the deferred filter scope from the original PRD.

choices.label: Total page views on the launch blog post
choices.explain: Vanity. Tells you about marketing, not product.

choices.label: Day-7 retention of users who tried the feature vs those who didn't
choices.explain: The clearest early signal that the feature added real value, not novelty.

hi-IN.title: Tier-2 cities mein DAU/MAU
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek Mumbai fintech ki kahani. Tier-2 cities mein launch hua. Founder bola — *'we have 2.4 lakh signups in 6 weeks!'* Investor khush.

PM ne dheere se data dekha. DAU/MAU = 0.08. **8 percent.** Matlab har 100 signed-up user mein se 8 actually app khol rahe the kabhi-kabhi. Founder ne kaha — *'leaky bucket nahi hai, growth hai.'* PM ne kaha — *'Sir, leaky bucket hai. Hum upar paani daal rahe hain, neeche se beh raha hai.'*

**DAU/MAU 0.18 se neeche B2B mein, aur 0.2 se neeche consumer mein, growth nahi engagement problem hai.** Vanity number bada hota hai, real number chhota.

en.title: When DAU/MAU exposes the leak
en.md:
Founders love to celebrate signups. 240,000 in 6 weeks sounds great in an investor update. The PM, who looked at DAU/MAU = 0.08, knows something different: out of every 100 signups, 92 are dormant.

DAU/MAU below 0.18 in B2B and below 0.2 in consumer is an engagement crisis dressed up as a growth story. Pouring users into a leaky bucket is the most expensive habit in early-stage product. Fix the leak before you celebrate the volume.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Feature Nobody Watched Die
blocks.source: Senior PM at Saral Books, a Bengaluru-based SMB accounting SaaS (~50K paying SMBs)
blocks.story:
On **September 19, 2023**, Saral shipped *'Smart Reconcile'* — an AI-powered bank-statement matching feature that had taken **9 engineer-weeks** and cost ₹6 lakh in vendor LLM credits to build. Launch day went perfectly: 600-word changelog, an in-product banner, a Twitter post that did **2.4K impressions**, and a launch dinner at Karavalli that ran ₹47,000 on the company card.

**Week 1**: 1,840 unique users tried the feature. The team toasted. The CPO Slack-emoji'd a rocket.

**Week 2**: 1,210 unique users. Slight dip but "normal post-launch settling."

**Week 3**: nobody pulled the dashboard.

The PM moved on to the next quarter's planning. Engineering moved on to a perf project. The growth team moved on to a paid-acquisition push. The dashboard stayed live but unloved.

In **March 2024 — six months later** — a new analyst joined and ran a routine feature-usage audit. *Smart Reconcile weekly actives*: **94 users**. Out of 50,000 paying SMBs. **0.18%**. The feature had quietly become a maintenance tax: 3 LLM-vendor invoices a month, 1 on-call page per fortnight, 0 measurable revenue impact.

The analyst's one-line slack: *"Did anyone ever look at this after launch?"*

Nobody had. The launch was a party. The follow-up was a Google Calendar invite that never got created.
blocks.takeaway: Shipping is the start of the experiment, not the end of the project. If nobody owns the 7-day, 30-day, and 90-day follow-up loops, the feature will die quietly and the company will pay the rent on its corpse for years.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Rhea's First Launch
blocks.setup:
**Week 11, Tarakash.** Rhea's first owned feature — the **Tally integration template** — is shipping in 5 days. Engineering is in QA. Design has done the in-product education. The growth team has a launch email queued.

Devika DMs her: *"Two things before you ship. (1) Have you done a pre-mortem? (2) What's your post-launch loop look like?"*

Rhea, in a moment of honesty, replies: *"…what's a post-launch loop?"*

Devika sends one emoji — the one that's a face with a slight smile and slightly closed eyes — and books a 30-minute room.

coach.name: Director-PM Devika
coach.role: Director of Product, Tarakash · once watched a feature she shipped die in production for 8 months before anyone noticed and she has not forgotten

stages.prompt: Devika starts: *"A pre-mortem is: imagine it's 30 days post-launch and the feature has flopped. Why?"* What does Rhea write down?

options.label: "It won't flop. We did good user research and engineering is solid."
options.explain: The point of a pre-mortem is to **assume failure** so you can spot blind spots while you can still act. "It won't flop" is the cognitive equivalent of refusing to buy travel insurance.

options.label: Five plausible failure modes: (1) CFOs don't discover the template in the integrations menu. (2) Tally OAuth flow breaks on Tally Prime vs Tally ERP. (3) Sample webhook payload doesn't match real invoice schemas. (4) First-run error messages are unclear so users churn after one bad sync. (5) Sales has no enablement so they don't tell trial customers it exists.
options.explain: **This is craft.** Five specific, addressable failure modes — not vibes. Now you can pre-empt 3 of these (discoverability, error copy, sales enablement) before launch. Devika says: 'You just saved yourself a re-launch.'

options.label: "It might flop because of unknown unknowns."
options.explain: Naming 'unknown unknowns' is just a fancy way of refusing to think. The whole point of the exercise is to convert unknowns into known concerns you can act on.

options.label: "It'll flop if engineering ships bugs."
options.explain: True but useless. Bugs are always a risk. A pre-mortem is for the **non-obvious** failure modes — discovery, education, second-order effects, integration edge cases. Pointing at engineering quality is not insight, it's blame-pre-positioning.

stages.prompt: Devika says: *"Good. Now — what's the **single metric** you're judging this feature on at day 7, 30, and 90?"*

options.label: Day 7: page views. Day 30: page views. Day 90: page views.
options.explain: Page views measure **curiosity**, not value. Saral's Smart Reconcile had 1,840 users in week 1 and was dead by week 3. Vanity metrics are how you celebrate features that are quietly failing.

options.label: Day 7: % of new trials that *attempt* a Tally sync. Day 30: % of new trials that *complete a successful first sync*. Day 90: % of new-trial **conversions** with at least one successful sync (the actual conversion-lift hypothesis).
options.explain: **Beautiful, layered metrics.** Awareness → activation → outcome. Each window measures a different stage and each can fail differently. If day-7 attempts are high but day-30 successes are low, you have an integration bug, not a discovery problem. Devika is now actively trying to hire-promote you.

options.label: Day 7, 30, 90: NPS.
options.explain: NPS is too noisy and too lagging for a single-feature signal. By the time NPS moves on a Tally integration, you'll be 6 months past the failure window. Pick action metrics, not sentiment metrics.

options.label: "I'll figure out what to measure once we ship."
options.explain: If you don't know what success looks like before you ship, you can't tell the difference between 'flop' and 'great' once you have data. Saral Books version of you, 6 months later: "did anyone ever look at this?"

stages.prompt: Devika asks: *"Last thing. What's actually scheduled in someone's calendar for the post-launch loop?"*

options.label: "I'll keep an eye on the dashboard."
options.explain: "Keep an eye on it" is the PM-equivalent of "the cheque is in the post." If it's not on a calendar with a name attached, it doesn't exist. This is exactly how Saral's Smart Reconcile died.

options.label: Three calendar invites, owned, dated: (1) **Day 7 review** — me + Shankar + growth, 30 min, look at attempt rate. (2) **Day 30 review** — me + Devika + sales, 45 min, look at activation + qualitative feedback from 3 trial users. (3) **Day 90 ship/kill decision** — me + Devika, 30 min, look at conversion lift, decide: double down, iterate, or sunset.
options.explain: **This is operational maturity.** Three forcing functions, three named owners, three dates, and crucially a **kill criterion at day 90**. The feature can't quietly outlive its usefulness. Devika literally pumps her fist.

options.label: A weekly Slack reminder to myself.
options.explain: Self-reminders get snoozed. Half-credit because at least it's something on a schedule, but without a meeting and named co-owners, it'll be the third thing you cancel during a busy week.

options.label: Day 30 retrospective only.
options.explain: One review window means you'll catch the wrong things at the wrong time. Day 7 catches discovery/launch bugs while you can still cheaply fix them. Day 90 catches whether the feature actually moves the metric. Skipping either is a different kind of expensive.

stages.prompt: **Day 90.** The Tally template hits **27% of new trials use it** and conversion is up from 11% → 16% (target was 18%). It's review time. What does Rhea recommend?

options.label: Sunset the feature — we missed the 18% target.
options.explain: 5 percentage points of conversion lift is enormous. Killing a working feature because it didn't hit the literal target number is missing the forest for the goalpost. Devika points out: 'A 45% relative improvement is not a flop.'

options.label: Double down — extend to Zoho and Quickbooks (2 of the original out-of-scope items from the PRD), and add a one-click 'detected your accounting tool' suggestion in onboarding to push attempt rate from 27% → 50%.
options.explain: **Yes.** The feature has a working signal — extend its reach (more accounting tools) and improve its top-of-funnel (smarter discovery). You also explicitly revisited the **out-of-scope** list from your original PRD because the data now justifies it. This is how good features compound.

options.label: Declare victory and move on.
options.explain: Saral's mistake. The feature is 27% adopted — there's still 73% of trials not using it. Moving on now leaves a 5-point gain on the floor when a 10-point gain is plausibly within reach.

options.label: Spend the next quarter rebuilding the feature from scratch with a 'better' UI.
options.explain: Premature rewrites are how PMs avoid the harder work of growing adoption. The current implementation works. The opportunity is **distribution and reach**, not a UI redesign.

outcomes.perfect: You ran a real pre-mortem, instrumented layered metrics, scheduled the loops, and made a defensible day-90 call. **Devika promotes you to PM at the end-of-quarter review** with the words: 'Most APMs ship and forget. You ship and learn.' That is the entire job.
outcomes.good: You got most of the operational rigor right but flinched on either metrics design or the day-90 decision. Re-read the section on **awareness → activation → outcome metrics** and the **ship/iterate/kill** decision tree.
outcomes.learn: You shipped the feature the way Saral shipped Smart Reconcile — to applause, then silence. Re-read the lesson, especially the parts on **pre-mortems**, **named-owner follow-up loops**, and **the day-90 kill criterion**. The launch is the easy part. The next 89 days are the job.

points: Ship-day is day 0, not day 30. The product question — did this work — opens at launch and stays open for at least 30 days.
Run a pre-mortem 1-2 weeks before launch: past-tense framing ('imagine it has already failed') produces 3-4x more risks than future-tense brainstorming.
Run the 7-day post-launch loop: day 0-1 fires, day 2-7 activation, day 7-14 retention delta, day 14-30 outcome verdict. Skip rows 3 and 4 and you're shipping coin flips.
If users who tried the feature have lower retention than users who didn't, the feature is actively hurting; investigate before you spend on adoption.
On day 30, write a 3-sentence verdict and share it. The PMs who do this consistently get promoted within 18 months; the PMs who don't keep shipping features into the void.

blocks.prompt: Pick a feature you (or your team) shipped in the last 90 days. Can you state, in three sentences, whether it worked? If yes — what evidence did you use? If no — what data would you need, and what would it cost to start collecting it now?

assessment.title: Product Management Fundamentals Assessment
assessment.description: Tests whether you can apply PM judgment across scoping, user research, prioritization, roadmapping, and launch. Most questions have one defensible right answer; a few have two. Read carefully — the wrong answers are wrong on purpose.

questions.stem: Your CEO forwards an email from your biggest customer asking for a 'simple feature — just let admins export user data to Excel.' What is the right first move?

choices.label: Open a JIRA ticket and forward it to engineering with the customer email pasted in.
choices.explanation: Translation is the PM's job. The engineer needs the why and the constraints, not a forwarded thread.

choices.label: Reply to the CEO with the three-question scope test: who, what change in their day, what happens if we do nothing.
choices.explanation: The scope test exposes whether this is one feature, three features, or a workaround for a different missing feature.

choices.label: Schedule a one-hour requirements meeting with the customer and three engineers.
choices.explanation: Premature. You don't yet know if this is worth an engineer's hour, let alone four.

choices.label: Estimate it yourself and put it on next sprint.
choices.explanation: Estimating something you haven't scoped is how 'just an export' becomes a six-week saga.

questions.stem: Which of the following count as outcomes (not outputs)? Pick all that apply.

choices.label: Reduce time to first invoice from 4 days to under 1 day
choices.explanation: Measurable change in user behavior. Outcome.

choices.label: Ship the new invoicing module by Q3
choices.explanation: Output. Says nothing about whether anyone uses it.

choices.label: Increase weekly active admins from 38 percent to 55 percent
choices.explanation: Behavior change with a number. Outcome.

choices.label: Launch a redesigned dashboard
choices.explanation: A redesign is a thing you ship; whether it moves a metric is the outcome.

questions.stem: You're interviewing a user who says 'I would absolutely use a dark mode if you built one.' What is the highest-signal next question?

choices.label: Great — what shade of dark would you prefer?
choices.explanation: Designs the feature before you've validated the problem.

choices.label: Tell me about the last time the current screen actually hurt your eyes or your work.
choices.explanation: Past behavior beats hypothetical preference. If they can't recall a moment, the demand is theoretical.

choices.label: On a scale of 1 to 10, how likely are you to use it?
choices.explanation: Stated intent is a known liar. The 9 becomes a 2 at launch.

choices.label: Would you pay extra for it?
choices.explanation: Pricing questions in a discovery call get polite nonsense.

questions.stem: Why does the 'silence move' work in user interviews?

choices.label: It makes the interviewer look thoughtful and senior.
choices.explanation: Optics, not signal.

choices.label: After a user finishes their first answer, three to five seconds of silence pulls out the second, more honest answer.
choices.explanation: The first answer is the social-acceptable one. The second is closer to the truth.

choices.label: It saves time on calls.
choices.explanation: It actually slows the call down on purpose.

choices.label: It avoids leading questions.
choices.explanation: Silence is unrelated to leading. The point is depth, not bias.

questions.stem: Which of these are red flags in a user interview transcript? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Every answer starts with 'I would' or 'I might'
choices.explanation: Hypotheticals. You want stories about what they actually did.

choices.label: User describes the last time they hit the problem with a date and a workaround
choices.explanation: Gold. This is exactly what you want.

choices.label: User suggests a specific UI solution within 2 minutes of the call starting
choices.explanation: Solution mode. Reset to the underlying job.

choices.label: User pauses for 4 seconds before answering a question
choices.explanation: Pauses are signal, not noise. They mean the user is actually thinking.

questions.stem: A PRD is best understood as:

choices.label: A specification document for the engineers
choices.explanation: Too narrow. Engineers are one audience. Sales, support, and future-you also read it.

choices.label: A contract with future-you about what 'done' means
choices.explanation: The PRD's job is to make 'done' unambiguous before the work starts. Future-you is the toughest stakeholder.

choices.label: A marketing brief for launch
choices.explanation: That's a launch plan, not a PRD.

choices.label: A wireframe with notes
choices.explanation: Wireframes are a tool inside a PRD, not the PRD itself.

questions.stem: You're using RICE to score 6 potential features. Feature A scores 800, feature B scores 720. Both have similar effort. The CEO is pushing for B. What does the framework actually tell you to do?

choices.label: Build A, the higher score wins.
choices.explanation: RICE is decision support, not a decision oracle. An 11 percent gap is within the noise of your own confidence numbers.

choices.label: Build B, the CEO's gut is the tiebreaker.
choices.explanation: Defaulting to HiPPO (highest-paid person's opinion) skips the actual question: what does the CEO know that your inputs missed?

choices.label: Treat the scores as a tie and decide on a non-RICE factor — strategic fit, dependency unlock, or learning value.
choices.explanation: When scores are within ~15 percent, the model is signalling 'these are equivalent; use judgment.' That's the point of decision support.

choices.label: Re-run RICE with stricter inputs until one wins.
choices.explanation: Tweaking the inputs to get the answer you want is how RICE becomes theatre.

questions.stem: What does the 'cut, don't compromise' rule mean in practice?

choices.label: Never reduce scope; ship the full thing or ship nothing.
choices.explanation: The opposite. The rule is about cutting features, not refusing to cut.

choices.label: When you must reduce scope, drop entire features rather than building half of every feature.
choices.explanation: Three good features beat six half-features. Half-features become support tickets.

choices.label: Compromise on quality before scope.
choices.explanation: Backwards. Scope flexes; quality doesn't.

choices.label: Cut deadlines, never features.
choices.explanation: Sometimes the deadline matters more than the scope. The rule is about how to cut, not whether to.

questions.stem: Why is a roadmap longer than one quarter mostly fiction?

choices.label: Engineers can't estimate that far out.
choices.explanation: True but secondary. Even with perfect estimates, the inputs change.

choices.label: User behavior, competitor moves, and your own learnings invalidate the assumptions every 6 to 10 weeks.
choices.explanation: A roadmap is built on assumptions about the world. The world's update frequency is faster than two quarters.

choices.label: Stakeholders forget what was on it.
choices.explanation: They don't, actually. They remember it word for word and quote it back at you.

choices.label: Deadlines slip.
choices.explanation: Slipping is symptom, not cause.

questions.stem: Which of these are valid uses of a roadmap? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Telling the same coherent story to sales, engineering, and the board
choices.explanation: Alignment is the primary job. One story, three audiences.

choices.label: Committing to ship feature X by month Y to a customer
choices.explanation: That's a contract. Roadmaps are not contracts.

choices.label: Showing the why behind your sequencing — not just the what
choices.explanation: If a roadmap is just a list of features, you've built a backlog, not a roadmap.

choices.label: Listing every JIRA ticket for the next year
choices.explanation: That's a backlog dump. Nobody reads past row 7.

questions.stem: Sales asks you to commit a feature to a prospect to close a deal. The feature isn't on the roadmap. What's the strongest first response?

choices.label: Yes, we can ship it next sprint.
choices.explanation: Whiplashed roadmap. Every other customer's feature just got bumped.

choices.label: No, it's not on the roadmap.
choices.explanation: Right answer, wrong delivery. Sales loses a deal and respect for product.

choices.label: Help me understand the deal — size, timing, and which 5 other customers want this. I'll come back tomorrow with a yes, no, or a swap.
choices.explanation: The polite no template. You're not refusing; you're moving to evidence-based decision.

choices.label: Add it to the backlog and move on.
choices.explanation: Hiding from a decision. Sales reads silence as agreement.

choices.label: A retrospective held before the project starts.
choices.explanation: Close, but a retrospective is about what happened. A pre-mortem is about what could go wrong.

choices.label: An exercise where the team imagines the launch failed and lists the most likely reasons, before shipping.
choices.explanation: Surfacing failure modes early, while they're cheap to fix, instead of later in the postmortem when they're expensive.

choices.label: A risk register filled in by engineering management.
choices.explanation: Risk registers are bureaucratic; pre-mortems are imaginative.

choices.label: A QA test plan.
choices.explanation: QA verifies known things; pre-mortem surfaces unknown things.

questions.stem: On day 7 after launch, which signals are most worth your attention? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Activation rate of users who reached the new feature
choices.explanation: Tells you if the feature is even discoverable and usable.

choices.label: Total page views on the launch blog post
choices.explanation: Vanity. Tells you about marketing, not product.

choices.label: Day-7 retention of users who tried the feature vs those who didn't
choices.explanation: The clearest signal that the feature added real value, not novelty.

choices.label: Number of internal Slack messages from sales about the launch
choices.explanation: Internal noise. Useful for politics, not for product decisions.

questions.stem: Your B2B SaaS has DAU/MAU of 0.18. Industry good is 0.4. Your CEO says 'great, lots of room to grow.' What's the more accurate read?

choices.label: The CEO is right; we're underpenetrated.
choices.explanation: DAU/MAU below 0.2 in B2B usually means you're a 'logged-in occasionally' tool, not a daily habit.

choices.label: We have an engagement problem, not a growth problem; new users won't fix what existing users won't do.
choices.explanation: Pouring users into a leaky bucket is the most expensive mistake B2B SaaS makes.

choices.label: DAU/MAU doesn't matter for B2B.
choices.explanation: It matters; the threshold is just lower than consumer.

choices.label: Switch to MAU/QAU.
choices.explanation: Hiding the problem behind a softer denominator.

questions.stem: You shipped a feature. Activation is good (60 percent of users tried it), but day-30 retention of those users is 8 percent lower than non-users. What does this most likely mean?

choices.label: The feature is great; users just need more education.
choices.explanation: When usage actively predicts churn, the feature is anti-value, not under-marketed.

choices.label: The feature is creating friction or false expectations; investigate before promoting it further.
choices.explanation: Negative correlation with retention is a stop signal. Find out why before you spend on adoption.

choices.label: Day-30 retention is too noisy to read; ignore it.
choices.explanation: 8 percentage points on a 30-day cohort is well above noise for most products.

choices.label: Retention will recover at day 60.
choices.explanation: Hope is not a plan.

questions.stem: An engineer says 'this will take 2 weeks.' Translated through PM judgment, the realistic ship date is roughly:

choices.label: 2 weeks
choices.explanation: Pure estimate, no buffer for the unknowns. You will be wrong.

choices.label: 3 to 4 weeks once you account for review, QA, edge cases, and one mid-project surprise
choices.explanation: The 1.5-2x rule on engineering estimates is empirical across most teams. Plan for it.

choices.label: 8 weeks; engineers always lie
choices.explanation: Cynicism, not judgment. Most estimates are honest, just optimistic about smooth paths.

choices.label: 1 week; engineers pad
choices.explanation: The opposite assumption is even worse. You'll commit to a date you cannot hit.

questions.stem: Which of these are the PM's job? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Deciding what NOT to build
choices.explanation: Saying no, with reasons, is more of the job than saying yes.

choices.label: Writing the production code
choices.explanation: If the PM is writing code, the engineering team is missing a person.

choices.label: Translating between users, engineers, sales, and leadership so each understands the others
choices.explanation: The translator role is the load-bearing wall of the job.

choices.label: Approving design pixel-by-pixel
choices.explanation: That's design's craft; PM weighs in on flow and tradeoffs, not pixels.

project.title: Capstone: The Sales-Forwarded Feature Request
project.prompt:
You are six weeks into your first PM role at **Tarakash**, a Bengaluru-based B2B SaaS that sells warehouse-management software to mid-market 3PL companies. Your VP-Sales, Vivek, forwards you this email at 9:47 PM:

> *Hey, urgent. Acme Logistics (₹38L ARR, second-largest customer, renewal in 11 weeks) wants 'a proper Excel export from the inventory dashboard, with filters and scheduling, plus a Hindi version of the UI for their warehouse staff in Lucknow.' Their COO said this is a 'must-have' for renewal. Can we get this on next sprint? — V*

It is Tuesday. Renewal conversations start in 4 weeks. Engineering is mid-way through a long-promised reliability sprint. The next planning meeting is Friday morning.

Write a **one-page response** (around 400-500 words) that you would send back to Vivek before the planning meeting. Your response must:

1. Apply the **3-question scope test** to break the request into separable pieces.
2. State which pieces (if any) you would commit to, which you would defer, and which you would refuse — with a reason for each.
3. Identify the **one user-research move** you would make in the next 48 hours to de-risk the decision.
4. Propose a **concrete next step** for Vivek, the engineering lead, and the customer — each with an owner and a date.

You may use bullet lists. Do not write a PRD. Do not promise dates you cannot defend. Write in the tone you would actually send to a VP at 10 PM — direct, calm, no jargon padding.

levels.label: Decomposes the request into distinct pieces; states a clear yes/no/defer for each with a reason; the VP could forward this email to the CEO without rewriting it
Identifies most pieces and takes a position, but reasoning is partially missing or buried
Treats the request as one undifferentiated ask, or hedges every position
Acknowledges Vivek's renewal pressure and the customer's underlying job; engages the engineering reliability sprint as a real constraint, not as an excuse
Considers one stakeholder well but dismisses or ignores another
Treats stakeholders as obstacles, or copy-pastes a 'no' template without context
Proposes a specific user-research move within 48 hours, names owners and dates for each next action, and gives Vivek something to send the customer by Friday
Has next steps but they are vague on owners, dates, or sequencing
Ends with 'let's discuss in the meeting' or no actionable steps

credential.title: Product Management Fundamentals
credential.description: Holder can scope a stakeholder ask, run a real user interview, write a one-page PRD, prioritize a backlog using RICE or value-vs-effort, build a now-next-later roadmap, and read post-launch metrics with judgment.
